# CHAPTER 212

## THE USHER

Antonius Vale found me before breakfast.

Not personally.

That would have been alarming.

A boy in a brown vest knocked while Lyssa was scraping the last beans
from last night's pot into a smaller bowl.

I opened the door.

He looked at me.

"Greg?"

"Usually."

He handed me a folded note.

"Vale."

Of course.

I stared at the note.

The boy held out his hand.

"For reply."

"I haven't read it."

"I can wait."

This was apparently a threat.

I opened it.

GREG,

YOUR DEBT REMAINS ACTIVE.

TABLE WORK.

DELIVERY ACCOUNTS.

TOMORROW, FIRST BELL.

ONE HOUR.

TRANSPORT FROM VALE OFFICE IF REQUIRED.

A. VALE

I read it again.

The debt had not changed while I was busy becoming a servant, nephew,
paper problem, and possible Guild criminal.

Rude.

Lyssa leaned against the table.

"Vale?"

"Yes."

"Debt?"

"Apparently."

"You knew."

"I knew quietly."

The boy was still waiting.

I looked at him.

"What reply does he need?"

"Yes or no."

"What happens if I say no?"

The boy shrugged.

"Then I bring back no."

Not a threat.

Worse.

Administration.

I turned the note over and wrote YES with Lyssa's charcoal.

Then added:

FIRST BELL IS OFFENSIVE.

I considered it.

Crossed that out.

Then wrote:

YES.

The boy took it.

"Tomorrow."

"Apparently."

He left.

I closed the door.

Lyssa put the smaller bowl in front of me.

"You thought he'd forgotten."

"I hoped his records had suffered."

"He's a lender."

"Records can suffer anywhere."

"Not there."

Probably not.

I ate cold beans.

The old arrangement had not survived my leg.

That part had been obvious.

Antonius had stopped treating me like a body he could send wherever a
body needed to go, which was considerate mostly because a missing leg
had made the alternative ridiculous.

The debt had survived.

So had the newer arrangement.

Table work.

Some room work.

No roads.

No pretending I could carry a warehouse because a ledger said I owed
somebody money.

I had done invoice comparisons for him before.

Two copper of debt credit.

Then nothing for a while.

Apparently Antonius did not require regular proof that a debt existed.

He had a ledger.

I hated that I could hear him saying it.

"Delivery accounts," Lyssa said.

"Yes."

"Carts?"

"Probably."

"Vale has carts."

"So does half Carrow."

"That is what makes it interesting."

"That is what makes it carts."

I ate another bean.

She went back to her work.

Nothing sat under the cup.

No Hessa note.

That one had already arrived.

Tomorrow had become crowded without asking me.

First bell, Antonius.

After midday, Hessa.

Theatre had not yet voted.

I left the Vale note on the table long enough to remember the time, then
folded it into my coat.

By third bell, the theatre cart still had its wheel.

The chalk mark still crossed pin and axle in one unbroken line.

Jori was crouched beside it anyway.

"Moved?"

"No."

"Then why are you there?"

"Checking."

"Didn't you just check?"

He looked at me.

I moved on.

Rinna had today's board in one hand and a short list in the other.

The short list was not theatrical.

BREN?

LEFT GLOVE.

CART YARD.

PAID ONCE. MORE.

That was all.

No strings.

No map.

No dramatic circle around the name.

Good.

She folded it before Pell could see.

I said, "Vale found me."

Rinna looked up.

"Who?"

"Antonius Vale."

That got recognition.

Not surprise.

"Creditor?"

"That is an ugly way to describe our relationship."

"Accurate?"

"Unfortunately."

"When?"

"Tomorrow, first bell. One hour."

She looked at the board.

I added, "Guild after midday."

"I remember."

"You told me to tell you."

"Now I remember twice."

"Efficient."

She looked at the board again.

"Tomorrow, Vale. Guild. Come after Guild if you're still useful."

"That's a very open condition."

"Then don't make it worse."

"So no morning theatre."

"No."

"Will you survive?"

"We did yesterday."

I had no answer to that.

Rinna pointed at today's board.

KING: MAREK / HARA / EVIN

LETTER BOX: VEYA / SELLEN / NESSA

SHORT: PELL / EVIN

GREG: HOUSE / SET

"No role?"

"No."

"Again?"

"You've had several."

"I've developed expectations."

"Kill them."

She handed me the ticket box.

Apparently today I was the usher.

I stood at the front door while the hall warmed behind me.

Pell and Jori argued over whether the rear cart being farther inside
made the passage safer or merely more annoying.

Nessa had three costumes hanging from the side rail.

Davin was repairing a lamp hook that had nothing to do with Havel.

Marek was eating something that smelled like garlic.

Normal.

A woman arrived first and paid for one.

Then two men together.

Then an older couple.

Then a broad man in a dark coat came up the street and looked directly
at the door.

My body noticed before my brain did.

Shoulders tight.

Good foot planted.

Crutch angle changed.

He stopped in front of me.

Large.

Dark coat.

No close-cut hair.

No glove.

He looked at the board beside the door.

"How much?"

I stared.

"For what?"

He stared back.

"The show."

Right.

"One copper."

"For both?"

"Each."

"That's robbery."

I almost laughed.

Did not.

"Then you may remain financially secure outside."

He frowned.

Then paid two copper.

His wife came up behind him carrying a wrapped bundle.

He had been waiting for her.

That was all.

I put the coins in the box.

The man said, "King first?"

"Yes."

"Good."

He went inside.

I watched his hands.

Both ordinary.

I disliked myself a little.

Rinna appeared behind me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Then sell tickets."

"That's what I'm doing."

"Do it less suspiciously."

"Apparently I have a face now."

"You've always had one."

Unfortunate.

Before the house opened fully, a familiar produce woman stopped at the
door with a basket on one hip.

She did not buy a ticket.

She pointed past me at Rinna.

"Her."

Rinna came over.

The woman said, "Your cart still inside?"

"Yes."

"Good."

Rinna waited.

The woman waited too.

Apparently Carrow had developed competitive waiting.

Finally the woman said, "Heard about Talla."

Rinna's face stayed flat.

"From?"

"Not your business."

"Then neither is mine."

The woman snorted.

"Fair."

She shifted the basket.

"No one came to me."

Rinna nodded. "Good."

I liked her.

She looked at me.

"Guild man?"

"No," Rinna and I said together.

The woman blinked.

"Fine."

She left without buying a ticket.

Rinna looked at me.

"That rumor is annoying."

"I agree."

"Do not improve it."

"I haven't."

"Keep doing that."

"Finally, a task suited to me."

She went back inside.

That was the entire threat for the afternoon.

A woman with turnips had heard something.

No new victim.

No new man.

No broken object.

The rumor remained small enough to fit in a produce basket.

I preferred it that way.

More people came.

A carpenter with sawdust on one sleeve.

Three young women who argued over who had paid last time.

A boy who tried to give me half a copper and confidence.

An old woman who said she would sit near the back because Marek
projected spit.

I did not verify this.

By the time the King started, we had twenty-six.

I counted twice.

Not because of scraping noises.

Because Rinna had made me count twice.

Progress could also be externally imposed.

I closed the door and carried the box back.

The King needed one platform, two chairs, the narrow table, and the red
cloth.

I brought the red cloth.

Wrong red cloth.

There were apparently two.

Nessa took it from my hand.

"Other."

"How many colors are secretly plural?"

"All of them."

I found the darker red cloth.

The first one belonged to Short.

No lesson.

The King started.

Marek was clean today.

Hara had a petition that was not upside down.

Evin had both shoes.

For several minutes, nothing improvised.

Then a fly landed on Marek's forehead.

He ignored it.

The fly remained.

Hara watched it.

The audience began watching Hara watching it.

Marek kept speaking.

Finally Hara said, "Your Majesty."

"What?"

"You have an adviser."

Marek's eyes narrowed.

"Where?"

Hara pointed at his forehead.

The audience laughed.

Marek held perfectly still.

"Is he wise?"

"He has stayed through the entire petition."

"Then wiser than most."

Bigger laugh.

Evin stepped closer, examined the fly, and said, "He disagrees."

"With what?"

"Everything."

The fly left.

Marek watched it go.

"Dismissed."

That was the strongest moment.

No chair moved.

No paper fell.

No one needed me.

Good.

Between pieces, I changed the table and nearly carried the wrong red
cloth back again.

Nessa made a sound.

I stopped.

"Right."

"Which?"

I looked at both.

"Darker stays."

"Good."

I carried the other.

Competence.

Letter Box played normally.

Veya found the key.

Sellen lied about a letter.

Nessa made the audience laugh by sitting down before Sellen finished
inviting her to sit.

The hall forgot about Bren because the hall did not know Bren existed.

I forgot for most of it too.

That was better.

At the rear, Pell whispered, "Vale?"

I looked at him.

"How do you know?"

"You said it near Rinna."

"I regret your hearing."

"Antonius Vale?"

"Yes."

"You owe him money?"

"Debt."

"That's money."

"Not currently."

"How much?"

"No."

He looked offended.

"Nessa gets to do that."

"Do what?"

"Say no when I ask how much."

"Learn from her."

"I refuse."

Short was next.

I moved the correct red cloth.

This was my contribution to art.

After the show, the broad man in the dark coat came back to the door.

My shoulders tightened again.

He held out a small wooden token.

"My wife dropped this."

I looked at the lost-things cup.

The matching token sat inside.

I handed it to him.

He nodded.

"Good show."

"Thank you."

"King was better last month."

"I'll tell him."

"Don't."

He left.

Ordinary people were exhausting.

Cleanup took longer because one bench had shifted enough to wobble on
the floor.

Davin fixed it with a thin scrap under one foot.

I did not ask whether this was another secret system.

I knew.

Jori checked the cart.

Chalk straight.

Rinna counted tickets.

One copper came to me.

Normal local pay.

I took it.

She said, "Tomorrow."

"Vale first bell. Hessa after midday. Then here if useful."

"Correct."

"You want me after Guild?"

"If Hessa says you can work."

"She'll say no lifting if I look tired."

"Then don't lift."

"What do I do?"

"We'll discover whether you have other skills."

"Harsh."

"Go."

I did.

At the pay table, I unfolded Vale's note again.

Rinna noticed.

"You're reading the same words."

"They may improve."

"They won't."

"Antonius writes efficiently."

"Then why read twice?"

"Hostility."

She took the note before I could stop her.

Not snatched.

Simply removed from my hand with the confidence of somebody accustomed
to props being in the wrong place.

"Delivery accounts," she read. "One hour."

"Private correspondence."

"You showed me the time."

"I showed you the time."

"Now I've seen the rest."

She handed it back.

"Debt credit?"

"Yes."

"How much?"

"Whatever the work earns against the debt."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the arrangement."

"How much debt?"

"No."

Rinna raised one eyebrow.

I had apparently learned Nessa's technique after all.

"Does Vale know about the men?" she asked.

"No."

"Are you going to tell him?"

"I don't know."

That answer bothered me because it was true.

Rinna folded today's ticket count.

"Don't tell him for us."

"I wouldn't."

"If it comes up, it comes up. But the hall didn't hire Vale."

"Vale would probably charge the hall for being rescued."

"Then definitely don't."

I put the note away.

That settled one thing.

If Antonius heard about Bren, it would not be because I marched into his
office and offered him the theatre's problem like an unpaid invoice.

On the way home I passed a Vale warehouse.

Not one I had worked in recently.

Two men rolled a barrel through the wide door while a clerk stood beside
a board and argued about a number.

A cart waited outside.

Its driver had one foot on the wheel hub.

I looked at the pin.

Present.

Of course.

Antonius's world was full of carts.

Warehouses.

Deliveries.

People who owed money.

People waiting to be paid.

People arguing over whether three jars had arrived broken or two.

Bren's world, as far as I knew, was two men at a theatre door and a
missing pin.

The overlap was not a connection.

It was Carrow.

That mattered.

I kept walking.

Lyssa was home before me.

She had changed out of the dark work wrap and was cutting the bad edge
off an onion.

Not my onion.

We had become onion-rich by accident.

"Vale?" she asked.

"Tomorrow."

"You didn't go?"

"Note."

"Ah."

I put the note on the table.

She read it.

"Delivery accounts."

"Yes."

"One hour."

"Yes."

"Transport covered."

"I can walk."

"That's not what it says."

"I know."

She gave me a look.

My leg had made certain arguments less philosophical.

"If he sends transport, use it," she said.

"I enjoy arriving under my own power."

"You enjoy being difficult."

"Also true."

She put onion into a pan with a little fat.

"What happened at theatre?"

"Nothing."

She waited.

"Actual nothing," I said. "Cart pin still there. Bren did not arrive.
Nobody threatened anyone."

"Good."

"There was a suspicious man."

Her hand stopped.

"He wanted tickets."

She resumed cutting.

"Greg."

"I discovered that."

"Before or after you stared at him?"

"During."

"Good."

"Why does everyone keep saying that?"

She ignored me.

I told her about the fly.

That got more interest than Vale.

Correctly.

Then I told her tomorrow's schedule.

"First bell Vale. After midday Hessa. Theatre after if I'm useful."

"That's three."

"Two and a possible."

"Still three places."

"Only if the third place wants me."

She put the knife down.

"Vale debt still alive."

"Yes."

"You knew."

"People keep emphasizing that."

"Because you keep acting surprised."

"I was surprised by timing."

"Why?"

"I've been busy."

"So has he."

That was fair.

Antonius Vale had not disappeared because I had joined a theatre.

My debt had not dissolved because Bren had walked through a door.

Hessa's paper did not care about either of them.

Tomorrow, I would spend an hour looking at somebody else's delivery
accounts, then sit behind glass and ask folded paper to move away from
me at two distances.

After that, if my arm still belonged to me, Rinna might find something
for me to carry without carrying it.

Lyssa put food down.

Onion.

Bread.

A little fat.

No beans.

"Luxury," I said.

"Eat."

I did.

The Vale note stayed beside Hessa's note.

One debt.

One experiment.

Neither had anything to do with Bren.

Probably.

I left it there.

The lamp burned steadily while we ate.

That was my household scale now: not wealth, not safety, just enough oil
that the room did not flicker every time the wick reconsidered its
profession.

I looked at the two notes again.

Lyssa said, "Stop."

"I wasn't touching them."

"You were thinking loudly."

I ate the rest of the bread.

Tomorrow could arrive without further preparation.

This was apparently allowed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 213

## THE COUNTER

Antonius sent a cart.

Not a carriage.

That distinction mattered because one had cushions and the other had a
sack of nails under the bench.

The boy from yesterday sat beside the driver.

He looked at my crutches.

"Vale said transport."

"I can walk."

"He said transport."

Lyssa stood behind me in the doorway.

"Get in."

I looked at her.

She looked at the cart.

I got in.

The sack of nails shifted under my good foot as we started.

Luxury.

Carrow at first bell belonged to people who had already decided the day
was late. Bakers had doors open. Carts occupied corners as if streets
had been built around them. A man carried three empty baskets on his
head and insulted somebody I could not see.

Vale's office was attached to one of the smaller warehouses, which meant
it was still larger than our room and contained fewer useful onions.

The driver stopped near the side door.

The boy said, "One hour."

"I remember."

He shrugged.

Apparently he was not responsible for whether I did.

Inside, a clerk pointed me toward the back table.

Antonius Vale sat there with three narrow stacks of paper and a cup he
was not drinking from.

He looked almost exactly as he had the last time I had seen him.

This was unreasonable.

I had lost a leg, joined a theatre, moved paper with mana, acquired
several kinds of employment, and accidentally convinced an extortionist
I might be dangerous.

Antonius had changed coats.

"I thought you'd forgotten me," I said.

"I have a ledger."

There it was.

I sat.

He looked at my crutches leaning against the chair, then at me.

"You move better."

"I've practiced."

"Walking?"

"Mostly falling less."

He slid the first stack toward me.

"You are harder to schedule."

"I have employment."

"You have several fragments of employment."

"That's still plural."

"Unfortunately."

The work was exactly what the note had promised.

Delivery accounts.

No hidden message.

No criminal code.

No secret list of men named Bren.

Three warehouse receiving sheets. Four cart departure tallies. Six
invoices. Two repair charges. One complaint from a customer who had
apparently believed a late barrel of lamp oil had ruined a wedding.

Antonius tapped the piles.

"These should agree."

"They don't?"

"If they agreed, I would not need you."

"Maybe you enjoy my company."

"No."

Good.

I started with dates.

Then cart marks.

Then loads.

The first disagreement was boring.

A clerk had copied the previous day's cart mark onto the next line. The
receiving record had the correct one because the driver had signed
beside it.

I put the two papers together.

"This is copied."

Antonius looked.

"Why?"

"Same mark two days. Different driver. The second receiving sheet has
the other cart."

"Which means?"

"Clerk copied yesterday before writing today."

"Probably."

"You don't sound impressed."

"I pay clerks to create fewer problems than they solve."

"I could create more."

"I know."

He made a small mark in his ledger.

The second problem took longer.

Three delivery invoices had deductions for late arrival.

Two matched the receiving times.

The third did not.

The invoice said the load arrived after second bell because of a wheel
repair.

The warehouse receiving sheet had it before first bell.

The repair charge existed.

Wrong day.

I spread the papers.

"This repair belongs to the next run."

Antonius looked at the repair slip.

"Why?"

"Cart mark."

"Same cart."

"Yes. But the repairman wrote the warehouse destination in the margin.
This one went south. The delayed invoice went west."

He took the slip.

The margin was faint.

"Useful."

"I prefer praise with more emotion."

"No."

He moved the corrected papers aside.

Most of the rest was ordinary mess.

A receiving clerk counted nine jars where the invoice said ten. A note
attached to the invoice said one jar had cracked while loading, which
solved the mystery unless the cracked jar had developed a commercial
afterlife.

A driver had written his own name differently on two sheets.

A repair charge for a wheel rim was real and correctly placed.

One late delivery was simply late because the driver had left late.

I found no conspiracy.

This was comforting.

Then I reached a receiving sheet marked for a yard near Mason's Cut.

I stopped.

Only for a moment.

Antonius said, "What?"

"Nothing."

"That was not nothing."

I looked at the sheet again.

It was not Talla's yard.

At least not the name she had given Rinna.

It was a receiving point two streets off Mason's Cut.

Ordinary.

"Place," I said.

"What place?"

"Mason's Cut."

Antonius waited.

I considered Rinna's instruction.

Do not tell Vale for us.

Fair.

"I am not bringing you a problem from the theatre."

"I did not ask for one."

"Good."

"Now tell me why you stopped."

I hated efficient people.

"Two men came to the hall."

Antonius's expression did not change.

"They wanted a small share."

"Of what?"

"Us."

"That is not an amount."

"Apparently it becomes one after you agree."

That got the smallest pause.

I continued.

"They mentioned Havel work. Said carts lose wheels. Lamps disappear.
Doors stop opening. Rinna refused."

"And?"

"Later somebody pulled the retaining pin from our handcart."

"Did you see them do it?"

"No."

"Then somebody pulled a pin."

"Yes."

He waited.

"Another cart yard near Mason's Cut got the same kind of visit," I said.
"They paid once."

"And?"

"More."

Antonius leaned back slightly.

"Of course."

"You say that like it's obvious."

"It is obvious after it happens."

That was annoyingly close to my opinion of plans.

"The man is probably called Bren," I said.

"Probably?"

"Someone at the other yard heard another man call him that."

"Bren what?"

"No surname."

"Then you have half a name."

"He has one glove."

Antonius looked at me.

"That is less than half a name."

"Left."

"Still."

"He may have something wrong with the hand."

"May?"

"I made him think I knew."

That finally changed Antonius's face.

Not much.

His eyes stayed on me a little longer.

"Why?"

"Because I didn't want him to break anything."

"Did it work?"

"He left."

"Then what?"

"He said he'd come back."

Antonius looked down at the delivery sheet.

"That is not the same as working."

"I know."

I did not tell him about the broom shadow.

Or Sellen's coat.

Or paper.

Especially paper.

He tapped the Mason's Cut sheet once.

"Did Rinna send you to tell me this?"

"No."

"Did she ask for help?"

"No."

"Do you?"

"No."

The answer came quickly enough that he looked at me again.

"I don't know what you would do," I added.

"Good."

"That sounded insulting."

"It was practical."

He stacked the Mason's Cut sheet with the others.

I said, "You don't care?"

"I care when people interfere with repayment."

I stared.

Antonius continued, "If the theatre pays you, and you pay me in labor or
coin, damage to the theatre can affect me."

"That is the nicest thing you've said to me."

"It was not intended kindly."

"Still counts."

"No."

I smiled despite myself.

He did not.

"Small share," Antonius said.

"Yes."

"After visible better work."

"Havel."

"And the other yard?"

"Good runs. Good coin."

He nodded once.

"The first amount tests whether payment is easier than refusal."

"And if they pay?"

"They have answered the question."

That was all.

No lecture.

No criminal map.

No revelation that Bren had once borrowed money from Antonius's cousin's
warehouse keeper.

Just arithmetic.

I looked at the papers.

"The cart yard paid once."

"And was asked for more."

"Yes."

"Then they answered clearly."

The clerk near the door called that first bell had passed.

Antonius checked the small sand timer on the table.

My hour was nearly gone.

He pointed at the corrected stacks.

"Two copper credit."

"Against the debt."

"Obviously."

"Cash would be more emotionally satisfying."

"You owe me."

"People keep remembering."

"I have a ledger."

"Yes."

He recorded the credit.

I did not see the remaining total.

I did not ask.

That felt like maturity or cowardice.

Possibly both.

As I stood, Antonius said, "If you get the other half of the name, tell
me."

"Why?"

"Because I asked."

"That isn't a reason."

"It is from this side of the table."

I put my crutches under me.

"Are you going to do something?"

"I have half a name and a story from my debtor about somebody else's
theatre."

"When you say it like that, it sounds weak."

"It is weak."

"Good."

"If it becomes relevant to my business, it may stop being weak."

There he was.

Not future Antonius.

Not yet.

But I could see the shape of the man who would eventually understand
that money moved through people before it moved through ledgers.

Or maybe I was cheating because I already knew.

"Do not make it relevant before it is," Antonius said.

I blinked.

"What?"

"Half a name. One story. Leave it there."

"That sounds like advice."

"It is accounting."

I left.

The Vale cart took me only as far as the central market because I told
the driver I had time.

He did not care.

Hessa's appointment was after midday.

I bought nothing.

This felt financially sophisticated.

At the Guild, the gray-coated woman saw me in the corridor.

"Paper Man."

"Comparative Paper Man."

She stopped.

"That is worse."

"I've been told."

Hessa had the same room prepared.

Same pale board.

Same chair mark.

Same glass.

Near remained marked.

Intermediate remained marked.

Far remained marked.

No one had improved the paper.

I sat.

Hessa looked at my hands.

"What did you do this morning?"

"Accounts."

"Physical."

"Sat."

"Before that?"

"Cart."

She looked up.

"Rode in one."

"Good."

"Lyssa made me."

"Also good."

"I dislike consensus."

She checked wrist rotation.

Fine.

Arm lift.

Fine.

Forearm.

Boring.

Shoulder.

Boring.

"Water?"

"Some."

She gave me more.

"This experiment has a lot of water."

"Your body continues to have a lot of water."

Apparently that joke had survived peer review.

She showed me today's page.

INTERMEDIATE / FAR.

AWAY ONLY.

SAME APPARATUS.

"We are not testing farther," she said.

"We are literally testing far."

"We are comparing the established intermediate position with the
existing far position."

"Which is farther."

"Do you want to go home?"

"No."

"Then be precise."

I drank water precisely.

She had already written the order on a folded slip and placed it face
down.

"You chose before I came?"

"Before you attempt."

"Why?"

"So I do not choose based on what happens."

That seemed unfair to outcomes.

She turned the slip.

INTERMEDIATE.

FAR.

FAR.

INTERMEDIATE.

"Four?"

"If your body stays boring."

"My body is deeply committed to boring."

"We will see."

Baseline first.

The thirtieth successful supervised minimal draw came without surprise.

The gathering was familiar now.

Small heat behind the sternum.

An inward pull that still felt less like grabbing something and more
like noticing a current already moving.

The wrist-side unevenness remained.

No increase.

No sudden reservoir.

No hidden second Greg.

Hessa watched.

"Enough."

I released.

She marked it.

Then the twenty-sixth supervised deliberate shaping attempt.

The gathered mana crowded toward the wrist side.

I tried to give it the rough deliberate form we had been using.

The shoulder wanted to join.

I lowered it.

The shape softened.

I did not chase.

It held badly for two breaths.

Then less badly for one.

Then it was gone.

Hessa wrote.

"Better?" I asked.

"Comparable."

"I miss praise."

"You have theatre."

Cruel.

External attempt thirty-one.

Intermediate.

Fresh matched fins.

Target and control.

Glass down.

Same chair.

Same foot.

Same hands.

Same request.

AWAY FROM GREG.

I gathered.

Shaped.

Kept it small.

Requested away.

Nothing.

Then the lower edge moved.

Tiny.

Clean.

Less than the width of my smallest fingernail.

Away.

Control unchanged.

Hessa checked.

"Response."

She wrote:

31. INTERMEDIATE.

TARGET DISPLACED AWAY.

SMALL.

CONTROL UNCHANGED.

I looked at Far.

She said, "Don't."

"I am allowed to look."

"Apparently not productively."

Fresh pair.

Attempt thirty-two.

Far.

The extra distance was not dramatic.

That was the annoying part.

The paper was still right there.

Reachable if I leaned.

Not reachable under the rules.

I gathered.

The shape was rougher.

I backed off.

Requested away.

Nothing.

I waited.

Nothing.

A shadow shifted.

I kept my head still this time.

Still nothing.

Hessa checked both fins.

"No observed response."

She wrote it.

I exhaled.

"Far remains rude."

"Far remains far."

"That was almost poetry."

"No."

Rest.

Water.

Hessa read another page while I sat with my hands open.

Someone outside asked for a frame.

Someone else said Soren had it.

A third person said Soren did not have it.

The frame developed a social life without us.

My forearm felt used.

Not tight.

Wrist fine.

Shoulder quiet.

Hessa checked anyway.

Then attempt thirty-three.

Far again.

Fresh pair.

Same everything.

I gathered.

The shape came cleaner at first.

Then tightened.

I let it become smaller.

Requested away.

For a breath, nothing.

Then the top edge turned.

Not much.

The lower corner shifted.

I stopped breathing.

Hessa leaned closer.

"Do not add."

I didn't.

The fin settled.

She checked from one side.

Then the other.

The target had moved.

Barely.

But the far corner now sat farther from me than it had.

The control had not changed.

Hessa looked at the marks.

Then at the paper.

"Observed."

My chest tightened for an entirely different reason.

"Far."

"One far response."

"Still far."

"Yes."

"At far."

"Yes."

I smiled.

She pointed at me.

"Do not make it larger."

"I haven't said anything."

"You are about to."

I was.

She wrote:

33. FAR.

SMALL ROTATIONAL RESPONSE.

NET DISPLACEMENT AWAY OBSERVED.

CONTROL UNCHANGED.

ONE OBSERVATION.

I read the last two words.

"You wrote that aggressively."

"I wrote it legibly."

Attempt thirty-four.

Intermediate.

Fresh pair.

My forearm was more obviously used now.

Still no pain.

Hessa made me rotate the wrist.

Fine.

Lift.

Fine.

"Last."

"I know."

"Say it."

"Last."

Same position.

Same request.

The gathering came.

Shape came rough.

I let it stay rough.

Requested away.

Nothing happened immediately.

Then the target slipped.

Small.

Straight enough that even I did not need to negotiate with the angle.

Away.

Control unchanged.

Hessa checked.

Then stopped the session.

No fifth attempt.

I did not ask.

This was growth.

Possibly.

She wrote for a while.

I drank water and tried not to turn one far movement into a kingdom.

Eventually she turned the page toward me.

30TH SUCCESSFUL SUPERVISED MINIMAL DRAW.

26TH SUPERVISED DELIBERATE SHAPING ATTEMPT.

INTERMEDIATE / FAR.

AWAY ONLY.

ATTEMPT 31, INTERMEDIATE: AWAY RESPONSE OBSERVED. CONTROL UNCHANGED.

ATTEMPT 32, FAR: NO OBSERVED RESPONSE. CONTROL UNCHANGED.

ATTEMPT 33, FAR: SMALL ROTATIONAL RESPONSE WITH NET DISPLACEMENT AWAY
OBSERVED. CONTROL UNCHANGED.

ATTEMPT 34, INTERMEDIATE: AWAY RESPONSE OBSERVED. CONTROL UNCHANGED.

Then:

INTERMEDIATE RESPONSE REPEATED.

FAR RESPONSE OBSERVED ONCE TODAY.

FAR RESPONSE NOT ESTABLISHED.

INTERMEDIATE REMAINS MORE RELIABLE THAN FAR UNDER CURRENT CONDITIONS.

DISTANCE DEPENDENCE REMAINS SUPPORTED.

NO RANGE ESTABLISHED.

NOT GENERALIZED.

I pointed.

"So it reaches far."

"No."

"It moved at far."

"Once."

"That is a response at far."

"Yes."

"So it reaches far."

"No."

I stared at her.

She stared back.

"Your problem," I said, "is language."

"My problem is you."

Fair.

"What can I say?"

"That a response was observed once at the far position in the current
apparatus."

"That sentence needs food."

"It is accurate."

"Paper moved farther away than before."

"Paper at the far position responded once today."

"Somewhat less close to me."

She considered.

"Still bad."

"Progress."

"No."

She repeated the restrictions.

All of them.

No independent draw.

No independent shaping.

No external testing.

No paper.

No coins.

No thread.

No larger objects.

No practice.

No loopholes.

No date for next session.

No next question yet.

"Body?"

"Forearm used."

"Wrist?"

"Fine."

"Shoulder?"

"Fine."

She checked.

"Non-lifting work is fine if it stays non-lifting."

"Theatre has discovered chairs."

"Then avoid discovering them."

I left with counts that had become:

thirty successful supervised minimal draws.

Twenty-six supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Thirty-four supervised external-effect attempts.

One far response.

Not far established.

Annoying.

Useful.

Both.

The afternoon house had already started when I reached the hall.

I checked the cart once.

Chalk straight.

Rinna saw me.

"Body?"

"Fine. No lifting."

She pointed at a stool beside the front table.

"Sit."

"I have become management."

"No."

There were six late arrivals during the next piece.

I took their copper.

One tried to argue the show was already partly over and therefore should
cost less.

I told him the remaining actors were still full size.

He paid.

Rinna heard.

She did not praise me.

I worked the front until the house ended.

No carrying.

No set.

No acting.

No Bren.

No broken pin.

No suspicious glove.

At close, Rinna gave me one copper.

I looked at it.

"For sitting?"

"For tickets."

"Vale gave me two copper credit for sitting."

"Go work for Vale."

"I owe him money."

"Then this seems difficult."

I took the copper.

At home, Lyssa had bread and a small bowl of cooked greens.

She looked at me.

"Vale?"

"Two copper off the debt."

"Good."

"Paper?"

"Four tries."

"How many?"

"Three responses."

She waited.

"Two intermediate. One far. One far did nothing."

"Far moved?"

"Once."

"Does that mean far works?"

I pointed at her.

"You've been talking to Hessa."

"No."

"It means a response was observed once at far."

Lyssa smiled.

I hated everyone.

"Theatre?"

"One copper."

"Bren?"

"No."

That was the whole day.

Debt moved.

Paper moved.

Tickets moved.

Bren did not.

For once, I was willing to count all four.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 214

## THE BROTHER

My forearm had become boring again.

This was good.

It was also rude after yesterday.

One piece of paper had moved at the far mark. Once. Hessa had spent
several lines making sure that one movement remained exactly one
movement, and my body had responded by becoming completely ordinary
overnight.

No ache in the wrist.

No shoulder complaint.

No mysterious new ability.

Nothing under the cup.

I checked once.

Lyssa was tying a narrow roll of pale cloth with blue thread.

"Nothing?" she asked.

"Nothing."

"You sound disappointed."

"I enjoy receiving instructions."

"No, you don't."

"Sometimes they prove people remember me."

She looked at me.

"Vale remembered you."

"That was debt."

"Still remembered."

I considered this.

"I preferred Hessa."

"Because she doesn't charge you?"

"She charges me dignity."

Lyssa put the cloth roll into her bag.

She had work near the west market, then somewhere beyond it. She did not
explain where. I did not ask.

This was becoming a skill.

She tore the last heel of bread in half and gave me one piece.

"Third bell?"

"Third bell."

"Bren?"

"Not scheduled."

"Good."

That was all.

She left.

I washed the cup.

I did not touch the paper under it.

At third bell, the theatre cart still had both wheels.

This was becoming how I greeted the building.

The cart sat farther inside than it used to, between the rear wall and a
stack of painted flats. Jori's chalk line across the replacement pin and
axle remained straight.

I looked.

I did not touch.

Pell was already beside me.

"Still there."

"Yes."

"I checked before you."

"Congratulations."

"I also checked the other wheel."

"Did it become dangerous?"

"No."

"Good work."

He nodded as if I meant it.

Marek came past carrying his King hat.

He held it with both hands.

Pell watched.

Marek stopped.

"Leave the hat alone."

"I didn't touch it."

"Keep that record."

Marek carried it backstage.

The King hat had apparently survived crime and become more valuable.

Rinna's board had three pieces.

EMPTY TABLE: VEYA / SELLEN / EVIN / GREG

WIDOW: HARA / NESSA / VEYA

SHORT: MAREK / PELL

GREG: BROTHER / SET

I pointed at Brother.

"Whose?"

Rinna looked up from a list.

"Veya's."

"In life?"

"In the play."

"Good. I wasn't prepared."

"You have six lines."

"Less prepared."

The Brother belonged to The Empty Table.

I had seen the role before, though not recently. He came in late,
complained that Veya's character had sent for him without saying why,
discovered that the family argument had already moved beyond him, and
left with somebody else's scarf.

The scarf was important.

Not emotionally.

It was simply the thing I had to remember.

Teren walked me through the entrance once.

"Door side. Not kitchen side."

"We don't have a kitchen side here."

"You still tried it last time."

"Memory is powerful."

"Use it on the correct entrance."

Nessa handed me a dull brown coat with a loose right cuff.

"This one."

I checked the label.

GREG.

"Mine."

"For today."

"Still counts."

She gave me the scarf.

Blue with a thin cream edge.

"Veya's chair. Then your hand. Then off."

"Why does he steal it?"

"He thinks it's his."

"Is it?"

"No."

"Good. Character depth."

Nessa left me.

The hall was normal.

Davin was checking a lamp bracket.

Jori was cutting two wicks to the same length and becoming angry that
one was not the same length.

Sellen and Evin were arguing over whether a written pause was actually
written.

Hara had brought a small paper packet of roasted seeds and was refusing
Pell access.

Nobody had been stabbed.

Nobody had burned anything.

Nobody had returned.

I was starting to believe the day might have poor dramatic instincts.

The knock came while I was moving the Empty Table table.

Not hard.

Three quick taps.

Rinna looked at the door.

So did everyone else.

That was new.

Before Bren, a knock had meant somebody wanted the door.

Now a knock had acquired options.

Rinna went herself.

She opened it only far enough to see out.

A boy stood there.

Maybe fourteen.

Maybe younger.

Thin arms. Dusty knees. A cord around one wrist. He held a folded piece
of rough cloth in one hand.

He looked past Rinna.

"Greg?"

Nobody moved.

The boy looked around again.

"One leg?"

Pell said, "That's him."

Rinna turned her head.

Pell looked offended.

"What? It is."

The boy held out the bundle.

"Man paid me to bring this."

Rinna did not take it.

"What man?"

"Said Bren."

The room got quieter.

Not silent.

Jori's knife still scraped once against wick.

Then stopped.

Rinna said, "You know him?"

The boy shook his head.

"Where did he find you?"

"South market."

"What did he look like?"

The boy shrugged.

"Man."

"Large?"

"Large enough."

"Coat?"

"Had one."

"Glove?"

The boy looked annoyed now.

"I didn't count his clothes."

Fair.

Rinna pointed at the bundle.

"What is it?"

"He didn't tell me."

"Did you open it?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"He paid me not to."

This was the first thing about the boy that made complete sense.

"How much?" Pell asked.

Rinna looked at him.

"What?"

Pell said, "Information."

The boy said, "One copper."

Pell looked impressed.

I was too.

The boy extended the bundle again.

"For Greg."

Rinna said, "No."

The boy stared at her.

"I have to give it."

"You can put it down."

"That's giving it."

"Fine."

He crouched and set it on the floor outside the door.

Then he remembered something.

"Bren says the share is still small."

Nobody answered.

The boy waited.

Rinna said, "Anything else?"

"No."

"Did he tell you to bring an answer?"

"No."

"Good."

She closed the door.

The boy's footsteps went away.

Pell moved first.

"One copper."

"The boy earned it," Rinna said.

Pell sighed.

Rinna waited a few breaths before opening the door again.

The bundle remained on the ground.

The boy was gone.

No one else stood immediately outside.

Rinna picked it up.

She did not hand it to me.

This seemed correct.

She put it on the front table and unfolded the cloth.

The iron pin inside was dirty.

Small.

Ordinary.

I knew what it was before Davin came over.

So did Jori.

Pell said, "That's ours."

"Probably," I said.

"He kept it."

"Apparently."

"That's rude."

Davin picked up the pin.

He turned it once.

There was a flattened mark along one side.

Jori leaned over.

"Nick."

Davin nodded.

I asked, "Certain?"

Davin looked at me.

"I made it."

"The first one?"

"Yes."

He set it beside the edge of the table.

Jori pointed to the nick.

"From the old axle edge. Before I cleaned it."

"So ours," Rinna said.

Davin nodded.

"Ours."

That changed the shape of things.

Not everything.

The boy had said a man calling himself Bren had paid him.

The boy had brought our missing pin.

The message had been about the share.

That was considerably less maybe than yesterday.

It was still not a surname.

It was not an organization.

It was not proof that Bren himself had pulled the pin with his own left
hand.

But somebody who wanted us to believe the message came from Bren had
possession of the pin.

That was enough to make my stomach feel colder.

Pell looked at the pin.

"He could have kept it."

"Yes," I said.

"Why give it back?"

Because the pin was not the point.

The point was that he had touched the cart.

The point was that he could prove it.

The point was that returning a cheap piece of iron cost him almost
nothing and made us imagine the next thing he might choose not to
return.

I did not say all of that.

Rinna folded the cloth over the pin.

"What do we send back?" I asked.

"Nothing."

I looked at her.

"Nothing?"

"Nothing."

"He addressed it to me."

"I noticed."

"That feels like it deserves something."

"No."

Pell said, "We could send his copper back."

"We don't have his copper," Rinna said.

"The boy does."

"Then especially no."

She carried the bundle to the small shelf near her papers.

The threat note was still there.

BREN?

LEFT GLOVE.

CART YARD.

PAID ONCE. MORE.

Rinna added one line beneath it.

PIN RETURNED.

MESSAGE IN BREN'S NAME.

She did not write BREN PULLED PIN.

Good.

I said, "Vale told me to tell him if I got the other half of the name."

Rinna looked at me.

"Did you?"

"No."

"Then don't."

"Bren returned a pin."

"Vale asked for a name."

"Yes."

"Good."

I disliked when everyone became Hessa.

Rinna turned away.

Then turned back.

"You made yourself part of this."

"I was already standing there."

"You made him think you were more than standing there."

I had no useful answer.

She was right.

The bluff had bought us time.

It had also apparently changed who Bren thought he was negotiating with.

I had wanted one man to hesitate.

I had not intended to receive mail.

Rinna pointed toward the stage.

"Table."

Right.

Theatre.

The Empty Table table was still halfway between the wall and where it
belonged.

I moved it.

Not alone.

Davin took the heavier end because Hessa had said no lifting yesterday
and because apparently I was now surrounded by people who listened when
told things.

We set it.

Teren checked the spacing.

"Too far left."

Of course.

We moved it six inches.

Crime could not protect me from furniture.

By the time the doors opened, the returned pin was off the front table.

The replacement pin remained in the cart.

The chalk remained straight.

The audience knew none of this.

They came in wanting seats.

One woman wanted to know whether Widow was playing.

A man with a red nose wanted the aisle.

Two boys argued over who had paid last time.

An older woman brought her own cushion and treated our bench as a
hostile surface she had prepared to defeat.

I worked front until Rinna sent me backstage.

My brown Brother coat waited on the hook.

The blue scarf waited on Veya's chair.

The pin waited somewhere near Rinna's papers.

I tried not to think about any of them.

The Empty Table began.

Veya and Sellen had the first exchange.

Evin came in with the letter.

The house was not large, but it was awake.

That mattered.

I stood in the wing.

Door side.

Correct side.

Teren touched two fingers together.

My cue.

I entered.

"You sent for me."

Veya looked at me.

"I sent for family."

"You should have been more specific."

A small laugh.

Good.

Sellen turned.

"Are you her brother?"

"Only when required."

Another laugh.

The written line after that was about the table.

I knew it.

I had known it ten minutes earlier.

Then I looked toward Veya's chair.

The scarf was there.

Blue.

Cream edge.

And for half a second the folded shape reminded me of the cloth around
the pin.

My line disappeared.

Not dramatically.

It simply ceased to exist.

Veya waited exactly long enough to make the audience think the pause
belonged to us.

Then she said, "My brother has always needed instructions."

There it was.

"Only the useful ones," I said.

Not the line.

Close enough to the scene.

Sellen said, "Then sit."

That got me back.

I sat.

The next written line arrived where it belonged.

No disaster.

No breakthrough.

Backstage, Teren did not say anything.

That was worse.

I remembered the scarf.

At least I did that.

Near the end, Veya threw it over the chair while arguing with Evin.

I picked it up.

"This is mine."

Veya said, "It is not."

"Then why do I recognize it?"

"Because you've stolen it before."

That was written.

I left with the scarf.

The audience laughed.

Backstage, Nessa took it from me.

"You missed."

"One line."

"I know."

"Teren knows."

"I know."

"Everyone knows."

"Probably."

Comforting.

Widow went next.

The strongest moment had nothing to do with us.

A little girl in the second row did it.

Hara stood near the front and asked Veya, "Do you expect me to believe
that?"

The line was rhetorical.

The girl answered.

"No."

The audience laughed before any actor did.

Hara stopped.

Looked at the girl.

Then back at Veya.

"Good. We have found one sensible person."

Veya turned toward the child.

"She's too young to understand."

The girl said, "No."

That was worse.

Hara put a hand to her chest.

Veya stared at the ceiling.

Nessa, who was supposed to cross behind them with a folded shawl,
stopped halfway and said, "Do you want her removed?"

The girl's mother was already laughing too hard to object.

Veya said, "No. She has earned her seat."

The whole house went.

The girl sat straighter.

Hara nearly lost the next line.

She got it back.

The scene continued.

Nobody backstage could do anything except wait until the laughter came
down.

Pell whispered, "Hire her."

Marek said, "No."

"Why?"

"She'll take my hat."

Pell considered this a serious concern.

Widow finished strong.

Short followed.

Marek and Pell did their usual work without a child taking over the
government.

Between pieces I passed Rinna.

"What was the line?" she asked.

I told her.

"Why'd you lose it?"

I looked at the shelf where the pin was no longer visible.

"Thinking."

"Do less."

"People keep recommending that."

"Listen."

Then she was gone.

Short got its laughs.

Pell missed one of his own cues because he was looking at the wrong side
of the room.

This improved my mood.

At close, the audience left with no idea that a piece of cart hardware
had occupied more of my attention than six written lines.

We swept.

We stacked.

Jori checked the replacement pin.

Chalk straight.

Davin checked the rear door.

Normal.

Nobody had taken a lamp.

Nobody had blocked the entrance.

No boy returned.

No Bren.

Rinna paid me one copper.

I looked at it.

"Still one."

"You forgot a line."

"I recovered."

"Veya recovered."

"Teamwork."

"One."

I took it.

Pell was still thinking about the returned pin.

"He paid a copper to return our own property."

"Yes."

"That's bad business."

"It wasn't a sale."

"He could have just brought it himself."

"No," Rinna said.

Pell looked at her.

She tied the small bundle closed again.

"He could have."

That landed differently.

Bren had chosen not to come through the door.

Maybe because he believed something about me.

Maybe because he doubted it.

Maybe because he wanted to see what we did.

Maybe because he had something else to do.

Those were all stories.

The only fact was that he had sent a boy.

Rinna put the pin away.

"We leave."

We did.

Not in one frightened knot.

Not alone either.

The company naturally broke into overlapping directions.

Marek and Pell went east for part of the route.

Veya and Nessa south.

I went west with Sellen until his turn.

No one followed that I could see.

I did not keep looking after every corner.

That was how you supplied your own extra men.

At home, Lyssa was later than me.

I had time to cut the remaining onion before she arrived.

This was dangerous because I was not good at cutting onions evenly.

She came in carrying an empty cloth bag and looked at the pieces.

"What happened?"

"To the onion?"

"To you."

Apparently my face remained a security failure.

"Bren sent the cart pin back."

She stopped.

"The missing one?"

"Davin says yes."

"Did Bren bring it?"

"No."

"Who did?"

"Boy. Runner, I think."

"He knows Bren?"

"Says a man called Bren paid him one copper in the south market."

"What did he say?"

"'The share is still small.'"

Lyssa put the bag down.

"To Rinna?"

"To me."

Her eyes came back to my face.

"Why you?"

"I don't know."

"You know some possibilities."

"Yes."

"Those aren't the same."

Everyone had become Hessa.

I put the onion in the pot.

"Rinna sent nothing back."

"Good."

"I asked."

"Of course you did."

"I thought maybe silence looked weak."

"Does it?"

"I don't know."

That was the problem.

I knew what I had said to Bren the first time.

I knew what Pell had put behind the panel.

I knew what Bren had seen.

I did not know what he had built from it.

Now he had sent something specifically to Greg.

Not the Guild man.

Not the gray coat.

Not Rinna.

Greg.

Maybe that meant he had learned enough to doubt the rest.

Maybe it meant he believed it more.

Maybe he wanted me to wonder.

Lyssa added beans to the onion.

"Vale?"

"No."

"You didn't tell him?"

"He asked for the other half of Bren's name."

"And?"

"I have a pin."

"Not a name."

"Exactly."

She nodded.

No Hessa note waited under the cup.

I did not check twice.

The counts remained thirty, twenty-six, thirty-four.

One far response remained one far response.

The theatre had both wheels.

The door still opened.

The lamps were still ours.

Bren had spent one copper to return a piece of iron worth less than the
message attached to it.

I had made him uncertain.

Now he was making sure I knew he was still there.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 215

## THE BAILIFF

Nothing happened in the morning.

This was becoming suspicious.

No runner.

No cart pin.

No note under the cup.

No one knocked on the door and asked whether I had reconsidered paying
criminals.

Lyssa had already left by the time I finished washing because a woman
near the west market had decided two repaired cuffs were not the same
length.

"They were the same length yesterday," Lyssa had said.

"Are they the same length today?"

"Yes."

"Then this seems easy."

She had looked at me for a long moment.

"You're very good with customers you don't have."

Then she left with the cuffs.

My body was ordinary.

Hessa had not summoned me.

Vale had not summoned me.

Bren had not summoned me.

For a few hours, nobody wanted anything.

I almost enjoyed it.

At third bell, the replacement cart pin remained exactly where Jori had
left it.

The chalk line was straight.

I looked once.

Pell came up beside me.

"You know we can both look."

"I know."

"You're making it feel competitive."

"Then lose."

He checked the other wheel.

I did not.

Growth.

The original pin was no longer on Rinna's shelf in plain sight. I knew
she had put it away somewhere with the little cloth bundle. I did not
ask where.

If Bren wanted us to think about it, making him work harder seemed
polite.

The hall smelled like dust, old paint, lamp oil, and something Hara was
eating out of a paper twist.

Nessa had two costume boxes open.

Jori had the rear door propped while Davin carried in a narrow painted
post.

Marek was wearing the King hat.

Pell looked at it.

Marek looked at Pell.

"No."

"I didn't move."

"You leaned."

"That isn't illegal."

"It is now."

Rinna was at the front table with a woman I had not seen before.

The woman wore a dark green overshirt over work clothes and had a narrow
leather purse hanging crosswise under one arm. Not rich. Not poor enough
to pretend money did not matter. She had ink on two fingers and a little
flour on one sleeve.

Rinna saw me.

"Greg."

I went over.

"This is Sera Venn."

Not Havel Sera.

Different Sera.

Carrow had apparently begun recycling names to save money.

The woman nodded.

"Venn is fine."

"Greg."

"I gathered."

She looked at my leg.

At least she did not say Guild.

Rinna said, "Venn keeps accounts for the Copper Kettle."

I knew the place.

Not well.

A tavern and eating room north of the market, wide front, covered side
yard, cheap stew, respectable beer according to people who drank more
beer than I did.

Venn said, "Owner's daughter is marrying a cooper."

"Congratulations to the cooper," I said.

Venn's mouth moved slightly.

"Maybe."

Rinna ignored me.

"They want entertainment after supper. Two pieces. Short. Covered yard
if weather holds, main room if not."

"When?" I asked.

"Tomorrow," Rinna said.

That got my attention.

Venn added, "Second bell after midday. Guests eat first. You play
after."

"How many?"

"Forty. Maybe fifty if cousins become real."

"How much room?" Rinna asked.

Venn described it with her hands.

Longer than our stage.

Narrower.

One support post in the middle of the covered yard.

Three tables that could move.

Two that could not.

No raised stage.

One side against a wall.

One side open to the lane.

Rinna asked about lamps.

Venn said they had six wall lamps and two hanging.

"Oil?"

"Ours."

"Benches?"

"Ours."

"Food?"

"Company eats after first piece."

That improved Pell's posture from across the room.

Rinna asked, "Payment?"

Venn looked at me.

Then at Rinna.

Rinna did not move.

Venn leaned closer and told her quietly.

I could not hear.

That was new.

Not secret enough to require another room.

Just not spoken across the hall.

Rinna asked two questions about when and who paid.

Venn answered.

Then Rinna said, "We'll do it."

I looked at her.

She looked back.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Say it."

"Are we taking the cart?"

Venn's eyes moved between us.

Rinna said, "We haven't decided."

Venn said, "You need it?"

"Maybe."

"We have stools."

"Not the same thing."

"Nothing is."

Venn gave Rinna a small folded paper with the tavern name, tomorrow's
time, and the owner's mark.

Then she left because she had actual work.

No ominous pause.

No strange glance toward the cart.

No secret Bren tattoo.

She just left.

Pell came over before the door finished closing.

"Food?"

"After first piece," I said.

"I heard."

"Then why ask?"

"I wanted confirmation."

Rinna unfolded the paper again.

Teren joined us.

So did Nessa.

Marek remained farther back because he was already dressed and had
discovered responsibility.

Rinna said, "Two pieces. Tomorrow. Copper Kettle."

Nessa asked, "Which?"

"King and Widow."

"Not Empty Table?"

"No."

Pell looked wounded.

"Short?"

"No."

"Why are we going?"

"Money."

That answered most theatre questions.

Teren asked about space.

Rinna repeated Venn's description.

Nessa asked about changing.

Small back room near kitchen.

Davin asked what had to travel.

That was when the conversation changed.

Not much.

Just enough.

Before Bren, the answer would have been a list.

Now Rinna looked toward the cart.

"Minimum."

Davin nodded.

"King platform?"

"No."

Marek said, "Good."

Pell said, "Coward."

"The floor exists," Rinna said. "Use it."

Nessa said, "Two costume boxes."

"One."

"I need two."

"One."

"Then someone wears their own trousers."

Pell looked down at his trousers.

"They're theatrical."

"No," Nessa said.

Jori asked, "Painted wall?"

Teren shook his head.

"Too much."

"Door?"

"No."

"Table?"

"The Kettle has tables."

Veya had come in without me noticing.

"Do their tables know the lines?"

"They'll learn."

Hara arrived behind her.

"Are we traveling?"

"Tomorrow," Pell said. "Food."

Rinna said, "Work."

"Food at work."

"Yes."

Hara accepted this.

I looked at the cart.

One costume box.

A prop basket.

Maybe lamps if the tavern's lighting proved bad, but Venn said they had
lamps.

No platform.

No painted wall.

No door.

They could probably hand-carry everything if enough people went.

Rinna was already counting.

"Davin?"

"Carry."

"Jori?"

"Carry."

"Nessa?"

"Costumes."

"Teren?"

"Front and space."

She kept going.

No guards.

No weapons.

No one proposed hiring six large men with matching sticks.

Just fewer things.

I said, "No cart?"

Rinna looked at Davin.

Davin said, "Don't need it."

Jori nodded.

"Not for that."

Rinna said, "Then no cart."

That solved one problem by leaving it inside.

"What about pay?" Pell asked.

Rinna looked at him.

"You'll know your share."

"When?"

"When I pay you."

"Can I know the company amount?"

"No."

"Could I guess?"

"You can do anything quietly."

Pell thought.

Marek said, "Don't."

"I haven't guessed yet."

"You're leaning."

Apparently leaning remained illegal.

Rinna tapped Venn's paper.

"We go together. We leave together. Nobody tells the street what they're
paying."

Hara opened her paper twist.

"Can we tell the street they're feeding us?"

"No."

"That's cruel."

"It's stew."

"You don't know."

"I know the Kettle."

That settled it.

Nobody said Bren.

Nobody needed to.

The cart stayed home.

The payment stayed between Rinna and the client.

The company would move together.

All of those choices could have been ordinary.

Yesterday made them less ordinary.

Rinna turned to today's board.

"Now stop doing tomorrow."

That was fair.

Today's board read:

DEBTOR'S UNCLE: EVIN / VEYA / SELLEN / GREG

KING: MAREK / HARA / EVIN

SHORT: NESSA / PELL

GREG: BAILIFF / SET

I stared at Bailiff.

"Am I collecting money?"

"No," Rinna said.

"Good."

"Why?"

"No reason."

Teren said, "You bring the notice."

"What notice?"

"The debt notice."

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

Neither of us said anything.

"That's unfortunate," I said.

"Five lines."

"More unfortunate."

The Bailiff entered halfway through Debtor's Uncle with a folded notice,
asked which man was responsible for the debt, was pointed toward three
different people, became increasingly irritated, and finally left the
paper with Veya because she was the only person who would take it.

I had seen Pell do it once.

Pell had played the Bailiff like a man personally offended by
handwriting.

Teren gave me a plain dark vest.

"No coat."

"Authority is shrinking."

"Good."

The notice was a folded sheet with meaningless marks.

Real paper.

No mana.

I held it normally.

This was not difficult.

We walked the entrance twice because today's stool sat where I wanted my
crutch.

The first time I clipped it.

The second time I moved around it.

Teren moved the stool two inches anyway.

"That was my solution."

"It was a bad solution."

"It worked."

"It made noise."

"Temporary applause."

"No."

The house came in normally.

No one asked for Guild.

No boy came back.

A Vale cart passed the open front while I was taking one copper from an
older man.

I recognized the painted side mark.

It continued down the street.

Nobody inside it noticed me.

Antonius existed without participating.

This felt healthy.

Debtor's Uncle started.

I waited in the wing with the notice.

Evin complained about the debt.

Sellen denied owing it.

Veya said the house owed everyone.

That got a laugh.

My cue came.

I entered without hitting the stool.

Professional.

"I have a notice."

Evin pointed at Sellen.

"For him."

Sellen pointed at Evin.

"For him."

I looked between them.

"Which of you is poorer?"

Veya said, "Yes."

Good laugh.

That was written.

I opened the notice.

There was nothing useful on it.

Also written.

"Someone owes twelve copper."

Evin said, "Then it cannot be me."

"Why?"

"I owe more."

That landed.

Sellen looked offended.

"Braggart."

I turned to him.

"Your name?"

He gave the wrong name.

I looked at the paper.

"That is unfortunate."

"Why?"

"I can't read this one either."

Small laugh.

The next part was simple.

I was supposed to hand the notice to Veya.

Instead, I handed it to Evin.

No Bren.

No threat.

No traumatic folded cloth.

I simply gave it to the wrong person.

Evin looked down at it.

Then at me.

Veya held out her hand.

I took it back from Evin and gave it to her.

"Administrative correction."

The audience laughed more than the line deserved.

Veya said, "Do I owe it now?"

"Apparently."

"Efficient."

We moved on.

Backstage, Teren said, "Veya."

"I found her."

"Eventually."

"Administrative process."

He walked away.

Normal failure.

Beautiful.

King went next.

The strongest moment belonged to a leaking cup.

Not a magical cup.

Not a prepared effect.

A bad cup.

Hara poured water into it before going on.

Nobody noticed the thin crack near the bottom.

Marek sat in the King chair.

Evin entered with the cup.

Set it beside him.

Water began creeping across the table.

Slowly.

Marek kept talking.

Hara saw it first.

She was supposed to accuse Evin of stealing a ribbon.

Instead, while Marek spoke, she moved the cup three inches toward him.

The water followed.

Marek noticed.

He moved it back.

Still speaking.

Hara moved it toward him again.

The audience started laughing before Evin understood why.

Evin looked at the cup.

Then at Marek.

"Your Majesty leaks."

Marek looked down at himself.

"I do not."

Hara pointed.

"Your table disagrees."

Marek lifted the cup.

Water dripped onto his sleeve.

He stared at it.

Then handed it to Evin.

"Arrest the cup."

Evin held it away from his body.

"On what charge?"

"Treason."

That broke the room.

Hara had to turn away.

Marek kept his face straight.

Mostly.

The cup continued leaking onto the floor until Davin reached from the
wing and took it during a crossing.

No one died.

The King survived.

The table required a cloth.

Short followed with Nessa and Pell.

Pell had spent the entire interval asking whether the cup would be
traveling tomorrow.

Nessa told him no.

He asked if the child from yesterday would be traveling tomorrow.

No.

King hat?

Marek said no from across the room.

Pell had become very easy to manage.

At close, Rinna paid me one copper.

Normal local day.

I put it away.

No danger pay.

No private-job money yet.

Tomorrow's work did not pay today.

This also felt healthy.

Then tomorrow invaded again.

Nessa packed the costume box.

One.

She was unhappy about it.

"Veya's second dress stays."

Veya said, "Good."

"You say that now."

"I hate that dress."

"You look good in it."

"I hate it attractively."

Nessa accepted this as possible.

Davin and Jori put together the prop basket.

No cart.

Teren wrote the two-piece order.

KING.

WIDOW.

Rinna checked the client paper again.

"Meet here before midday," she said. "We walk from here."

Pell asked, "How long?"

"Long enough."

"Food?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Do not tell anyone what they're paying."

"I don't know what they're paying."

"Excellent."

The cart remained inside.

Jori checked the replacement pin anyway.

Chalk straight.

He caught me watching.

"Still there."

"I know."

"You want to check?"

"No."

He looked disappointed.

Apparently my restraint was ruining community.

We left in the usual pieces.

Nothing happened.

No runner.

No lookout I could prove.

No man in a heavy coat waiting at the corner.

No one asked where we were playing tomorrow.

I passed a produce stall and bought two small carrots because they were
cheap and because Lyssa had recently demonstrated that food could
contain colors other than brown.

At home, she had not returned yet.

I cut the carrots more evenly than yesterday's onion.

This was progress nobody would record.

Lyssa came in after dark enough that I had started the beans.

She put her bag down harder than usual.

"Same length?" I asked.

"Yes."

"Did she agree?"

"Eventually."

"What changed?"

"I measured them in front of her."

"Were they the same?"

"Yes."

"So the measuring changed nothing."

"It changed her."

That sounded familiar.

She washed her hands.

"Your day?"

"New job tomorrow."

She looked over.

"Outside?"

"Copper Kettle. Wedding. Two pieces."

"Late?"

"Probably not very. We go after midday. Food."

"Cart?"

"No."

The question came immediately.

Before Bren, I was not sure it would have.

"Don't need it," I said. "One costume box. Prop basket. Tavern has
tables and lamps."

"Pay?"

"Rinna knows."

"You don't?"

"No."

"Good."

I looked at her.

"Why is that good?"

"Because you talk."

"Only when necessary."

She looked at me.

"Sometimes while asleep."

"Unverified."

She tore one carrot piece from the board.

"Bren?"

"Nothing."

"Pin?"

"Still with Rinna. Replacement still in cart."

"Vale?"

"Passed one of his carts."

"Did it rescue you?"

"No."

"Bad cart."

"Hessa?"

"Nothing."

She ate the carrot.

"Then wedding."

"Wedding."

It was good work.

That was the problem.

Not because work was dangerous.

Because good work was visible.

Havel had been visible.

The cart yard's good runs had been visible.

Tomorrow we would leave the hall carrying costumes and props and come
back after feeding fifty people laughter for money.

The easiest answer would have been not to go.

Rinna had not even seriously considered it.

Neither had I.

We needed the work.

More than that, the company wanted it.

Bren had asked for a share of something we had not earned yet.

Tomorrow we were going to earn it anyway.
