# CHAPTER 218

## THE PAYER

The copper was still in the fold.

I checked.

This was unnecessary.

I checked anyway.

Lyssa was standing with one arm inside a dark green sleeve that did not
belong to her. The rest of the dress lay across the table.

"You think it escaped?"

"No."

"Then why are you checking?"

"I have an appointment."

"With the copper?"

"Antonius."

"Does Antonius know?"

"About the appointment?"

"The copper."

"No."

She pulled the sleeve through and inspected the seam.

"Then the copper is having a more stressful morning than Antonius."

Probably.

Nothing waited under the cup.

No Hessa note.

My forearm was boring. My shoulder was boring. My wrist was boring.

Thirty, twenty-six, thirty-four.

Paper remained paper.

Money had become the strange thing.

I ate bread.

Lyssa left before me because the shoulder-seam problem had turned into a
second fitting. I had no idea whether this meant the first fitting had
failed or succeeded.

"Which?"

"Both."

"Useful."

"Customer work."

She left.

I waited until first bell after midday because arriving early to inspect
my own debt felt too much like enthusiasm.

The west Vale office occupied the front corner of a warehouse that
smelled of dust, rope, old wood, and whatever had leaked into the floor
over several years and become part of the building.

Two carts stood outside.

One Vale side mark.

One without.

Men were moving sacks through the larger door. A clerk argued with a
driver about six barrels that were physically present and apparently
administratively absent.

Commerce.

I went through the smaller door.

The young woman with the narrow ledger case sat at a side desk.

"Gregory."

"Greg."

"Still."

"Apparently."

She pointed toward the inner room.

"He's waiting."

"That sounds threatening."

"He has another appointment."

Worse.

Antonius sat behind a table with three ledgers open.

Not one.

Three.

I stopped in the doorway.

"You've made my debt plural."

"No."

"Then why are there three books?"

"Because you made your debt inconvenient."

"That sounds like blame."

"It is accounting."

He pointed to the chair.

I sat.

The chair had a straight back and one leg slightly shorter than the
others. I discovered this immediately.

Antonius watched me rock once.

"Don't."

"Fix your chair."

"It's a guest chair."

"That explains your business relationships."

He slid the first ledger toward himself.

I could see my name.

GREGORY.

"Greg."

"The debt is Gregory's."

"I am Gregory."

"Then we've resolved something."

I disliked him.

Good.

The page was older than I expected.

Not ancient.

Just handled.

Marks had been added in different inks. Dates. Credits. Charges.
Cross-references to other pages. Several entries pointed into the second
ledger.

I leaned closer.

"How much?"

Antonius looked at me.

"That was fast."

"I have theatre."

"Of course you do."

He put one finger on the first line.

"Your original loan."

The amount was there.

I stared.

Then the next line.

Additional financing.

Then another.

A fee.

Another advance.

A correction.

Gambling stake.

Materials.

Something I had apparently agreed to while believing future income would
solve present arithmetic.

That version of me had been very optimistic.

"Why isn't there one number?"

"There is."

"Where?"

"At the end."

"Then why are we doing this?"

"Because you asked what you owe."

"I meant the number."

"No. You asked what you currently owe. If you only wanted the number, my
clerk could have copied it."

I looked at him.

He was right in the most annoying possible way.

I went back to the page.

Thirty-five percent.

Eight days.

The original terms were still there.

Then later financing with different conditions attached.

First refusal language.

Labor conversion after default.

Credits for work.

Charges I remembered.

Charges I did not.

I pointed at one.

"What's that?"

"Additional advance."

"For?"

"You were short."

"That describes a period."

Antonius opened the second ledger.

There.

A date.

A note.

I remembered.

"Oh."

"Useful?"

"No."

"It cost money."

"Apparently."

The problem became clear after several minutes.

The ledger was real.

The debt was real.

The exact current balance was also in the ledger.

But the manuscript of my own life had been financially incompetent.

Not literally.

The problem was that several old advances and gambling periods had been
recorded through linked entries, and I did not remember the numbers well
enough to pretend I had always carried the total in my head.

Antonius did.

Of course.

He tapped the current balance.

I looked at it.

Large.

Not impossible.

Those were different things.

I could not reduce it to normal theatre days cleanly because it crossed
denominations and my world had never bothered to give me a comforting
conversion table.

That was probably healthier.

I could still understand scale.

One copper for an ordinary theatre day.

Two copper from the Copper Kettle.

Two copper of debt credit for an hour of useful Vale account work.

Silver had mattered enough that six of them once covered two days of
Pell's time.

Gold belonged to another altitude entirely.

My debt had pieces from the period when I had treated future success
like a currency.

Now I was earning copper.

Regularly.

That was better than earning theories.

It was also slower.

"Well?" Antonius asked.

"I liked it better when it was abstract."

"Most debtors do."

"Do they start theatre companies?"

"You did not start the theatre company."

"Good. I was worried the ledger had added that."

He leaned back.

"You've begun earning."

"Some."

"Regularly."

"Mostly."

"And now the debt bothers you."

"It bothered me before."

"No. Before, it offended you."

I looked at him.

He continued.

"You treated it as an obstacle."

"It is."

"Now you're treating it as an account."

I hated that more because it sounded accurate.

"Do you rehearse these?"

"No."

"That was too neat."

"You are not complicated."

"Fuck you."

"There."

Normal.

I looked down again.

There were the two recent credits.

The earlier post-injury invoice comparison.

Two copper.

The delivery-account reconciliation.

Two copper.

Separate lines.

Small.

Real.

I touched the second one.

"You actually wrote it."

Antonius stared at me.

"What did you think credit meant?"

"I knew."

"Apparently not."

"I knew conceptually."

"Excellent. My favorite kind of repayment."

I took the little cloth fold from inside my shirt.

Antonius looked at it.

I put one copper on the table.

He looked at the copper.

Then at me.

"One."

"Yes."

"This is not a strategy."

"No. It's a copper."

His mouth moved slightly.

Not a smile.

Accounting amusement.

"Do you intend to do this every day?"

"No."

"Good."

"Can I?"

"Yes."

"Do you want me to?"

"I want the debt repaid."

"Helpful."

"I do not care whether a given copper came from theatre, a private
performance, or you selling your remaining leg, provided the transaction
is lawful and you remain capable of producing more value."

I looked at him.

"That became dark."

"Don't sell the leg."

"Thank you."

"It would damage repayment."

There he was.

He pulled the copper toward the ledger.

The clerk entered without knocking, carrying a small ink pot and a
narrow receipt strip.

Apparently one-copper payments had infrastructure.

Antonius made the entry.

Cash.

One copper.

Date.

Account.

The clerk copied it.

Antonius signed.

She handed me the strip.

I stared at it.

"That's it?"

"What were you expecting?"

"Nothing."

"Then you're satisfied."

I folded the receipt.

The current balance had changed by one copper.

Not emotionally.

Mathematically.

That was enough.

"What should I pay?" I asked.

Antonius closed one ledger.

"Whatever does not make you useless."

"Very precise."

"You have variable income."

"Yes."

"You have household expenses."

"Yes."

"Your theatre work may disappear."

"Optimistic."

"Private work may increase."

"Maybe."

"Your Guild work currently produces no meaningful cash."

"Correct."

"Your labor for me can reduce the account when I have work that suits
you."

"Yes."

"Then why would I invent a fixed payment that either becomes trivial
when you earn more or cripples you when you earn less?"

I stared at him.

"You're refusing to budget for me."

"I would rather die."

"Good."

"Pay when you have surplus. Work when I have suitable work. Do not
starve yourself to improve my ledger."

"Lyssa said that."

"She is protecting you."

"You're not?"

"I'm protecting the ledger."

Distinct.

Useful.

I folded the receipt smaller.

"Anything else?"

Antonius looked at the clock on the wall.

"You have theatre."

"That's not an answer."

"It is twenty-two minutes."

"You scheduled twenty."

"You spent two arguing with a chair."

"The chair started it."

He stood.

Meeting over.

I stood too.

At the door he said, "Greg."

I turned.

"If you want the figure again, ask for a copy of the balance. Do not
schedule me to discover that numbers remain numbers."

"You're welcome."

"For?"

"The copper."

"Get out."

I did.

I walked to the theatre with a receipt in my pocket.

The debt had not become small.

It had become finite.

That was worse in one way.

Better in another.

Impossible things did not require plans.

Finite things did.

Third bell was already approaching when I reached the hall.

The cart sat inside.

Chalk straight.

Replacement pin installed.

I checked once.

Rinna was moving names on the board.

"Vale?"

"Still rich."

"You?"

"Less indebted."

"How much?"

"One copper."

She stopped.

"You went there to pay one copper?"

"I went there to learn the account."

"And paid one."

"Yes."

"Did he laugh?"

"Not visibly."

"Strong restraint."

I looked at the board.

KING.

EMPTY TABLE.

SHORT.

GREG: SERVANT / SET.

I pointed.

"I've been Servant."

"So has Evin."

"That isn't how titles work."

"What titles?"

"Nothing."

Nessa threw the dull brown coat at me.

I caught it badly.

"Servant."

"Apparently."

The role was the same small role from before.

Four lines.

Carry a folded cloth.

Answer one question.

Leave.

Normal.

I liked normal.

We were halfway through setting the King table when the front door
opened.

Not knocked.

Opened.

Jori had not latched it yet.

The close-haired man in the heavy coat stepped inside.

Bren.

Probably Bren.

Same spokesman from the first night.

Left glove.

Same way of holding that hand closer to his body.

One man remained outside.

Not the narrow man from the Copper Kettle as far as I could know.

I had never seen that man.

This one I knew.

My stomach dropped before my thoughts caught up.

Nobody screamed.

Pell stopped carrying a stool.

Marek's King hat was in his hands.

He did not put it on a broom.

Progress.

Bren looked at me first.

"Greg."

Rinna stepped between the front table and the open floor.

"You're talking to me."

Bren's eyes moved to her.

Then back to me.

Then her.

"Wedding went well?"

Nobody answered.

That landed harder than a threat.

Copper Kettle.

He knew.

Not necessarily how.

Not necessarily from the thin man.

But he knew.

Rinna said, "What do you want?"

"The same thing."

"We answered."

"You didn't."

"We did."

Bren looked around the hall.

Not theatrically.

Counting.

People.

Doors.

Work.

Maybe value.

"The share is still small."

Rinna waited.

Bren said, "One copper."

I almost laughed.

Not because it was funny.

Because I had just put one copper on Antonius Vale's table.

One copper.

Antonius had given me money in the past.

Loaned it.

Advanced it.

Attached terms.

Recorded labor.

Recorded credit.

I owed him because value had moved toward me first.

Bren wanted the same coin for having shown up twice and stolen a pin.

The coin did not care.

I did.

Rinna said, "No."

That was it.

No speech.

Bren looked at her.

"One."

"No."

"Cheaper than a wheel."

Davin's face changed.

Rinna's did not.

"You returned the pin."

Bren smiled slightly.

"Did I?"

Evidence.

There.

He did not confirm he pulled it.

Did not confirm who did.

Only that he knew what she meant.

Rinna said, "We're not paying you."

Bren looked at me.

"You agree?"

Rinna said, "You're talking to me."

He ignored her for one second too long.

That was probably deliberate.

I could feel the old impulse.

Say something strange.

Use the glove.

Use Mason's Cut.

Use Guild.

Use the receipt in my pocket.

Make him build a larger story.

I had no better truth than last time.

So I did not.

"I don't own the theatre," I said.

Bren studied me.

That was true.

Boring.

Useful.

"Didn't stop you before."

"No."

Rinna said, "It stops now."

Bren looked at her again.

Good.

The room had changed.

The first night I had made myself larger because we needed thirty
seconds of uncertainty.

Now that false size had become a business problem.

Rinna was cutting it back down.

Bren said, "You took the Kettle job."

"Yes."

"You'll take others."

"If they pay."

Pell shifted.

Rinna did not look at him.

Bren said, "Then one copper is small."

Rinna said, "No."

His jaw tightened.

Not much.

There.

He had expected negotiation.

Maybe.

Inference.

He glanced toward the rear.

Jori stood there.

Davin near the scenery.

Veya had come from behind the hanging cloth.

Hara beside her.

Nobody had weapons.

Nobody needed to pretend.

Bren said, "Next time won't be one."

Rinna answered, "Then this was the cheap time to say no."

That was almost clever enough to sound rehearsed.

It probably was not.

Bren looked at her.

Then me.

"Greg."

I said nothing.

He waited.

I still said nothing.

That felt harder than the first bluff.

Finally he turned.

At the door he stopped.

"Good crowd at the Kettle."

Then he left.

The man outside went with him.

No attack.

No broken lamp.

No hand on a knife.

Just street noise swallowing two men.

Rinna shut the door.

Jori latched it.

Nobody moved for a moment.

Then Pell said, "I liked him better as a runner."

Rinna turned.

"He was never the runner."

"You know what I mean."

"I do. That's why I'm correcting you."

I sat on the nearest bench.

My leg was fine.

My good hand was not shaking much.

Progress.

Or delayed shaking.

Teren came from the rear.

"Are we canceling?"

Rinna looked at the door.

Then at the board.

"No."

Teren nodded.

"Then set."

That was theatre.

We set.

King went first.

I was not in it.

Marek missed a word because Pell had moved the King's cup six inches.

Marek found the cup, stared at Pell from the stage, and changed his line
to, "Even my servants now tax me."

Pell whispered from behind the cloth, "That's not me."

Hara heard him.

"It speaks."

The audience laughed.

Marek said, "Worse."

That beat belonged to them.

Good.

Empty Table followed.

My Servant role came after.

Four lines.

Brown coat.

Folded cloth.

I entered on the correct side.

Veya asked, "Did you bring what I asked?"

I held up the cloth.

"I brought what I was given."

"Is it what I asked?"

"I was not given that information."

Small laugh.

Written.

Useful.

No one in the audience knew a man had demanded one copper before house.

I did not miss a line.

I did not improve one.

I did the job.

After the Short, Rinna paid me one copper.

I looked at it.

She saw.

"Keep that one."

"Why?"

"You paid Vale?"

"Yes."

"This one feeds you."

That was not an order.

It sounded like one.

I put it away.

Jori checked the cart before we left.

Straight.

Davin checked the rear.

Fine.

Nothing missing.

Bren had come.

Bren had left.

The building remained a building.

We went home in overlapping groups anyway.

Lyssa was not home when I arrived.

I put the Vale receipt on the table.

Then moved it because oil and receipts seemed incompatible.

She came in later carrying a paper-wrapped bundle and looking pleased.

"Good day?"

"Paid."

"For?"

"Two alterations and a rush repair."

"How much?"

She looked at me.

"Money face."

"Sorry."

She put the bundle down.

"Your day?"

I showed her the receipt.

She read it.

"One copper."

"Yes."

"You paid it."

"Yes."

"How much do you owe?"

I told her what the ledger had shown me.

Not because the exact figure suddenly fixed anything.

Because now I knew.

Her expression changed slightly.

"That's a lot."

"Yes."

"Payable?"

I thought.

"Yes."

Not quickly.

Not cleanly.

Not without food and oil and broken things and days when theatre paid
nothing.

But yes.

Then I told her Bren came back.

She stopped unwrapping the bundle.

"Actually Bren?"

"The man from the first night. Same close hair. Same left glove. He
answered to Bren before. I still don't have a surname."

"What did he want?"

"One copper."

Lyssa looked at the receipt.

Then at me.

"You paid Vale one."

"Yes."

"And Bren wanted one."

"Yes."

"Different."

"Very."

"What did Rinna say?"

"No."

"Then?"

"He said next time won't be one."

Lyssa was quiet.

"Did he touch anyone?"

"No."

"Break anything?"

"No."

"Follow you?"

"Not that I saw."

"Did you do the thing again?"

"What thing?"

She looked at me.

"The stupid impressive thing."

"No."

That hurt.

"Good."

"I told him I don't own the theatre."

"True."

"Painfully."

She finished opening the bundle.

Inside were two small rolls and a piece of smoked meat.

I stared.

"Paid and fed?"

"Customer's mother."

"Your work is improving."

"My customers are."

We ate.

The Vale receipt stayed on the table.

One copper less debt.

One copper Bren had not received.

Same amount.

Different arithmetic.

Outside, somebody laughed in the street.

A cart rattled past.

Nothing happened.

For tonight, that was enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 219

## THE PURCHASER

The receipt survived the night.

So did I.

Both seemed worth noting.

I put the little strip of Vale paper inside the box where Lyssa kept
needles, two buttons that did not match anything we owned, and a piece
of blue thread she claimed was too useful to throw away.

"Why there?" she asked.

"Because you know where it is."

"I know where most things are."

"Exactly."

She was tying back her hair with a strip of cloth while looking at a
pale sleeve on the table.

"That is not a filing system."

"It is now."

She gave me the expression that meant she had decided not to improve me
before breakfast.

Nothing waited under the cup.

No Hessa note.

My arm was normal.

My shoulder was normal.

My wrist was normal.

Thirty, twenty-six, thirty-four.

I ate the last of one roll with a little smoked meat and tried not to
think about money.

This lasted almost a full bite.

One copper to Vale.

One copper Bren had wanted.

One copper Rinna had paid me after the show.

I still had to eat.

Lyssa had been correct.

Antonius had also been correct, which was more irritating.

"You're doing the numbers again," Lyssa said.

"I'm eating."

"Poorly."

"I paid a debt yesterday."

"You paid one copper."

"That is how paying works."

"Yes. Slowly."

She picked up the sleeve.

"I have to take this back before the woman decides her shoulder changed
overnight."

"Can shoulders do that?"

"Customers can."

She left first.

I went to theatre at third bell.

The front door was open.

That was normal.

The shouting was not.

Not dangerous shouting.

Rinna shouting.

Different category.

"I ordered two tins."

A boy stood just inside the door with empty hands.

He looked approximately thirteen and deeply interested in being
somewhere else.

"I know."

"And wicks."

"I know."

"Where are they?"

The boy glanced at me as if I might be able to explain adulthood.

I could not.

"Master Olin said not to bring them."

Rinna stared.

Behind her, Jori had three lamps on the worktable with their caps off.

One was nearly empty.

Another had enough oil for a show if we did not believe in long endings.

The third had oil but a wick that looked like it had lost faith.

Nessa was sorting costumes.

Pell was eating something.

Of course.

I checked the cart once.

Replacement pin installed.

Chalk straight.

Then I went back to the argument.

Rinna said, "I ordered them yesterday morning."

"Yes."

"Cash on delivery."

"Yes."

"I have cash."

The boy looked miserable.

"I know."

"Then what changed?"

"Master Olin said not to bring them."

Rinna took a breath.

"What did Master Olin say?"

"That was it."

"Did he say why?"

The boy looked toward the street.

"Someone told him you weren't good for it."

Rinna became still.

Not frightened.

Still.

"Good for what?"

"Payment."

"I pay on delivery."

"I know."

"Does Olin?"

"Yes."

"Then what exactly was he told?"

The boy swallowed.

"That your money was spoken for. That there was trouble over it. Master
Olin said he wasn't getting in the middle."

Nobody said Bren.

That mattered.

I thought Bren.

That mattered less.

Rinna said, "Who told him?"

"I don't know."

"Did you see?"

"No."

"Did Olin?"

"I think."

"Think?"

"He talked to him."

"Today?"

"Early."

"At the shop?"

"Yes."

Rinna looked at Jori.

"How much do we have?"

Jori pointed.

"Enough for King if we cut the front lamps and don't burn the rear one
until house. Not enough for both pieces unless we get more."

"What are we playing?"

Teren answered from the board.

"King. Letter Box."

Rinna looked at the boy.

"Tell Olin I am coming to speak with him."

The boy's relief was immediate.

"Yes."

He left.

Rinna turned to me.

"You're coming."

"Why?"

"You walk."

"Questionable."

"You also heard what he said."

"Better."

She looked at the board, then at Jori.

"Can you hold setup?"

"Yes."

"Nessa?"

"Yes."

"Pell?"

Pell swallowed.

"Probably."

"Don't."

"I didn't do anything."

"Keep doing that."

We left.

The oil shop was not far.

Far enough to make the missing tins annoying.

It sat on a narrow market street with a painted yellow drop above the
door and a smell that made every spark in Carrow feel personally
interested.

Tins lined the rear wall.

Wicks hung in tied bundles.

A squat man with gray in his beard was arguing with a woman about lamp
smoke.

He saw Rinna.

His expression changed.

Not fear.

Regret.

Good.

"Rinna."

"Olin."

The woman looked between them, decided she had purchased enough lamp
smoke for one morning, and left.

Olin wiped his hands on his apron.

"I was going to send word."

"You did."

"I mean proper word."

"You sent a boy with no oil."

"I didn't want him carrying it if there was going to be trouble."

Rinna put both hands on the counter.

"There is no trouble between you and me."

"I know."

"Then why don't I have my oil?"

Olin looked at me.

"Who's this?"

"Greg."

His eyes went down.

Leg.

Back up.

Recognition, maybe.

Not personal.

Rumor had done work before.

Rinna said, "He heard your boy."

Olin sighed.

"A man came in."

"What man?"

"I don't know."

"Name?"

"No."

"What did he say?"

"Asked if I supplied the theatre."

Rinna waited.

Olin continued.

"I said sometimes. Oil. Wicks. Small things. He said I should be careful
taking promises from you because other people had a claim on the money."

"We don't buy on promise."

"I know."

"Did you tell him that?"

"Yes."

"What did he say?"

Olin rubbed his beard.

"That cash can disappear before it reaches a counter."

I felt something cold settle under my ribs.

Rinna did not move.

"Description."

"Thin fellow. Brown coat. Dark hair."

I looked at Rinna.

She looked at me.

Neither of us said Copper Kettle.

Olin noticed.

"You know him?"

"No," Rinna said.

Correct.

"Have you seen him before?"

"No."

Also correct.

The Copper Kettle worker had.

Not us.

Rinna said, "Anything else?"

"Not old. Narrow face. Talks quiet."

"Gloves?"

I asked.

Rinna turned her head.

I stopped.

Olin thought anyway.

"Don't remember."

Fine.

Rinna said, "Did he threaten you?"

"No."

"Ask you not to sell to us?"

"Not exactly."

"What exactly?"

"He said if I wanted to keep my money, I shouldn't have goods walking
toward people whose money belonged somewhere else."

"That's not exactly subtle."

Olin shrugged.

"I don't know your business."

"You know how I pay you."

"Yes."

"Have I failed to pay you?"

"No."

"Then you do know that part of my business."

Olin's mouth tightened.

"I don't need trouble for two tins of oil."

There it was.

Not loyalty.

Not betrayal.

Two tins of oil.

A merchant did not need to love Bren to become useful to him.

He only needed to dislike uncertainty.

Rinna asked, "Will you sell me the order now?"

Olin hesitated.

"Cash now."

"It was cash on delivery."

"Cash here."

"Same price?"

Another hesitation.

That one irritated me more.

"Olin."

"I had to send the boy twice."

"You sent him once."

"He came back."

"From my theatre."

"That's twice walking."

Rinna stared.

Olin sighed.

"Same price."

Good.

He brought out two tins and a tied bundle of wicks.

Rinna counted the money onto the counter.

I watched.

I could not help it.

Coins had become louder.

Olin took them.

Then Rinna said, "We need another small tin."

Jori had not asked for another.

Olin knew it.

"So you don't have to come back tomorrow?"

"So I don't have to find out tomorrow whether someone else has told you
my money belongs to him."

Olin looked uncomfortable.

"That costs more."

"Yes."

He named the amount.

Rinna looked at me.

"How much do you have?"

I stared.

"This feels like a trap."

"How much?"

I had the copper from yesterday.

Other money existed.

I was not reconstructing my purse in a lamp-oil shop.

"Enough for the small tin."

"Buy it."

"Company expense?"

"Yes."

"Recorded?"

She looked at me.

"Vale ruined you in one meeting."

"Record it."

"I will reimburse you."

Good.

I put my copper on Olin's counter.

Not the Vale copper.

That one was already gone.

This one had been theatre pay for less than a day.

Now it was lamp oil.

Olin pushed the small tin toward me.

Money became objects very quickly when allowed.

Rinna took the wick bundle.

I carried the small tin.

She carried one larger tin.

Olin came around the counter with the other.

"I'll send this."

Rinna looked at him.

"With who?"

"My boy."

"Fine."

Olin paused.

"If the man comes back?"

"Tell him nothing about what I buy, what I pay, or when."

"That's easy."

"And send me word."

Less easy.

Olin frowned.

"I don't want in this."

"You're already in it enough to cancel my delivery."

That landed.

He looked at the tins.

Then at Rinna.

"If he comes back, I'll send word."

"Good."

We left.

On the street I said, "Thin face. Brown coat."

"Yes."

"Dark hair."

"Yes."

"Same description as the Kettle."

"Yes."

"So."

"So the descriptions match."

I waited.

Rinna kept walking.

"That's all?"

"That's what we know."

"He asked about the cart. Then the money. Now he talks to Olin."

"If it's the same man."

"Olin's description matches."

"Yes."

"You're exhausting."

"Carry the oil."

I did.

At the theatre, Jori received the tins like we had returned from war
carrying medicine.

"How bad?"

Rinna handed him the wicks.

"Annoying."

"Cost?"

"Normal order plus another tin."

Jori looked at me.

"Why are you holding it like it insulted you?"

"I paid for this one."

Rinna said, "Company did."

"Eventually."

She reached into her purse and gave me a copper.

I looked at it.

"That was fast."

"I don't want you developing a heroic relationship with lamp oil."

"Too late."

I put the copper away.

The transaction had lasted less than half an hour.

My money had left.

Company money had returned.

Oil remained.

Accounting.

I understood Antonius slightly better and resented him for it.

Rinna gathered Teren, Jori, Nessa, Veya, and Davin near the worktable.

Not a council.

They were the people standing closest who mattered.

She told them exactly what Olin had said.

No embellishment.

Pell drifted closer.

Rinna pointed at him.

"You can listen if you don't improve it."

"I never improve anything."

Marek, from behind him, said, "Correct."

Rinna ignored both.

"For now, if a supplier gets told we don't pay, they check with me
before changing an order. If somebody asks about private jobs, payment,
carts, or what we carry, they get nothing useful. I'll tell Venn. Talla
already knows enough to send word if she hears the same thing."

Greg, I thought.

Do something.

This was something.

Small.

Boring.

Useful.

I said, "What about other suppliers?"

"I'll speak to the ones we actually use."

"Today?"

"The ones I can."

"I can carry notes."

Rinna considered.

"After set."

Good.

Not investigation.

Work.

We set.

King first.

The extra oil meant the lamps burned normally.

Nobody in the audience knew they had almost been darker because a thin
man in a brown coat had said something in an oil shop.

That was probably how most functioning things worked.

A dozen small failures prevented before anyone noticed.

I had no role in King.

I worked the rear cloth and moved one stool.

Letter Box gave me a tiny part Teren had added to the board while I was
gone.

MESSENGER.

Three lines.

Of course.

I had already been Messenger once.

The universe lacked title discipline.

I complained.

Teren said, "Then don't put it on a chapter."

I stared at him.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I wore no coat.

I carried a folded letter.

My job was to enter, hand it to Sellen, say the recipient was not home,
answer one question, and leave.

Before that, the King had its best moment.

One of the front benches had developed a squeak.

Not a dangerous squeak.

A conversational one.

Every time a broad man near the end shifted his weight, the bench
answered.

Marek was in the middle of accusing Hara's petitioner of changing her
story.

"You said there were three."

Squeak.

Hara looked toward the bench.

"There were."

"You said four yesterday."

Squeak.

Hara said, "My witness has arrived."

The broad man froze.

The audience laughed.

Marek looked at him.

"Does he always testify like that?"

The man carefully shifted.

Squeak.

Hara folded her hands.

"Only under pressure."

That got them.

Marek let the laugh finish.

Then he said, "Remove the witness."

The broad man lifted both feet slightly off the floor.

The bench went silent.

Hara said, "Intimidation."

Bigger laugh.

Marek lost the corner of his mouth for half a second.

Strongest moment.

Not mine.

Good.

Letter Box started after a short reset.

My entrance came clean.

I handed Sellen the folded letter.

"The house was empty."

"Did you knock?"

"Yes."

"How many times?"

"Enough to become suspicious."

Small laugh.

Written.

"Did anyone answer?"

"No."

"Then why are you suspicious?"

"Because I was still there."

Another small laugh.

I left.

Adequate.

No miracle.

No Bren.

No brown coat in the house that I could prove mattered.

Afterward, while Nessa packed costumes, Rinna gave me three folded
notes.

One for a cloth seller.

One for the woman who occasionally repaired lamp glass.

One for Venn at the Copper Kettle.

"What do they say?"

"None of your business."

"I'm carrying them."

"Then carry them."

"Are they threatening?"

"No."

"Poetry?"

"No."

"Debt confessions?"

"Greg."

I took the notes.

The cloth seller was closest.

She read Rinna's note, snorted, and said, "You pay me."

"Apparently that is now news."

"If someone tells me otherwise, I'll ask."

Good.

The lamp-glass woman was not there.

Her son took the note.

I did not interrogate him about thin men.

Growth.

The Copper Kettle was busier.

Venn stood near the front counting mugs.

She read the note.

Her face tightened.

"Same man?"

"Maybe."

"What happened?"

I told her the narrow version.

Oil delivery canceled.

Olin described thin face, brown coat, dark hair.

Venn nodded slowly.

"That sounds like him."

"Sounds."

"Yes."

Good.

Everyone had become Hessa.

Terrible.

Venn folded the note.

"If he comes back, I'll send someone."

"Rinna said don't tell him anything useful."

"I already didn't."

"Continue being excellent."

She looked at me.

"Do you want a beer?"

"Is it free?"

"No."

"Then I want it less."

I left.

Back at the theatre, Rinna was still there.

So were Jori and Davin.

The cart chalk remained straight.

The replacement pin remained installed.

No one had broken anything while I carried notes.

I reported.

Cloth seller would check.

Lamp-glass note delivered to son.

Venn said Olin's description sounded like the same man she had seen.

Rinna wrote one line on her small paper.

KETTLE / OLIN DESCRIPTION MATCHES.

Then another.

SUPPLIERS CHECK WITH US.

That was all.

No: BREN'S MAN.

No: LOOKOUT.

No: GANG.

I pointed.

"You could write 'probably.'"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because the paper survives us being stupid."

That was annoyingly good.

"Did Hessa teach you that?"

"No."

"She'd like you."

"Don't threaten me."

We closed.

I earned one copper for the show and the work around it.

Rinna did not pay extra for walking oil through Carrow.

I considered filing a complaint.

Then remembered she had reimbursed the oil.

At home, Lyssa was trimming loose thread from a shoulder seam.

Different dress.

Different shoulder.

Apparently the city was coming apart one upper arm at a time.

"How was theatre?" she asked.

"Expensive."

She looked up.

I told her about the canceled oil delivery.

The man.

Olin.

The description.

The extra tin.

The notes.

Lyssa listened.

"Did Bren tell Olin not to sell to you?"

"No."

"Did the man say Bren?"

"No."

"Same man as the Kettle?"

"Venn thinks the description sounds like him. Olin says thin face, brown
coat, dark hair."

"So maybe."

"Yes."

She cut a thread.

"How much did it cost?"

"More than one copper would have."

"That doesn't make paying Bren cheaper."

"I know."

I did.

Talla's yard had paid once.

Then more.

One copper was not the price.

It was the first answer.

Still, I hated that refusing it had already cost real money.

Oil.

Time.

Walking.

Attention.

Three notes.

A supplier who had become uncertain enough to cancel an order he knew we
paid for in cash.

Bren had not needed to break anything today.

Maybe Bren had not done anything today.

That distinction remained.

I hated that too.

Lyssa put the dress aside.

"What are you going to do?"

"Rinna already did something."

"What?"

"She told the businesses we actually use to check with her instead of
listening to strangers."

"Good."

"I carried notes."

"Heroic."

"I carried oil too."

"Then they'll sing about you."

"They should."

She smiled.

I ate bread.

No note came from Hessa.

No runner came from Bren.

No one knocked.

The theatre had spent more than one copper refusing a one-copper demand.

It had also opened, performed, paid people, bought oil, and told its
neighbors how to reach it.

That was not winning.

It was work.

For now, work was action.
# CHAPTER 220

## THE LANDLORD

I bought bread on the way to the theatre.

This should not have required a decision.

It did.

The baker named the price. I paid it. He gave me bread. Nobody congratulated me for preserving my ability to remain alive while owing Antonius Vale money.

Progress.

I also bought a small cake of soap because ours had become a translucent insult beside the basin. That hurt more.

Bread was food. Food was defensible.

Soap felt optional right up until I remembered Lyssa leaning away from my shirt the previous evening and saying, "You work in a theatre full of people."

She had not actually said I smelled.

She had created a structure in which I could reach the intended conclusion.

Theatre was corrupting everyone.

I put the soap in my coat, hung the bread from one crutch in a cloth bag, and continued west.

No Hessa note had been under the cup that morning. No magic. No symptoms. Nothing new in my right arm, hand, shoulder, residual limb, or phantom foot. Thirty draws. Twenty-six deliberate shaping attempts. Thirty-four supervised external attempts. One far response observed once and not established as anything more useful than that.

The numbers stayed where they were.

Good.

The theatre did not.

A boy was waiting outside when I arrived.

Not one of ours.

Olin's delivery boy.

He recognized me first.

"You're the oil man."

I stopped.

"I carried one tin."

"Oil man."

"I have done other things."

He shrugged.

I looked at the open front door.

"Why are you outside?"

"Woman's busy."

That could describe Rinna at every hour I had known her.

Inside, someone was dragging a bench across the floor. Jori was on a ladder adjusting a lamp bracket. Nessa had a green coat spread over two chairs and was arguing with Pell about whether a tear had existed yesterday. Marek stood onstage holding a wooden cane and looking deeply pleased with himself.

Normal.

Good.

The boy said, "Master Olin sent me."

That changed the morning.

I looked at him again.

"The man came back?"

"Yes."

"Brown coat?"

"Yes."

"Thin face?"

"Yes."

"Dark hair?"

"Yes."

"Quiet?"

The boy thought.

"Not loud."

Better answer.

"Did Olin tell you to tell me?"

"He said tell the woman."

"Excellent."

I moved aside and pointed through the door.

"Let's find the woman."

Rinna was in the rear passage counting folded handbills while Davin tried to convince her that twelve and fourteen were different numbers for a reason.

"They are both enough," she said.

"For different streets."

"People can walk."

"That is not how handbills work."

"Then make more."

Davin looked at me.

"Help."

"No."

"Coward."

"Olin sent word."

Rinna stopped counting.

The boy appeared behind me.

She put the handbills down.

"What happened?"

The boy told it badly.

That was not criticism. He was thirteen and had apparently been sent across Carrow because an adult merchant did not want to leave his shop. He started with the man coming in, skipped to Olin getting angry, returned to a question about oil, forgot whether the man had touched the counter, remembered he had not, and then explained that Master Olin had said not to answer anything.

Rinna did not interrupt until he finished.

Then she asked, "What did he ask? Exact if you can."

The boy looked at the ceiling.

"If you bought the oil."

"How?"

"He said, 'She bought it anyway?'"

Rinna nodded once.

"Then?"

"Master Olin said he doesn't talk about customers."

"Good."

The boy looked surprised by the praise.

"Then he asked if you paid cash."

"Exact?"

"I think, 'She paid cash for it?'"

"What did Olin say?"

"Same thing. Customers."

Rinna glanced at me.

I said nothing.

The boy continued.

"Then he asked if you were still doing shows. Master Olin said if he wanted a handbill he could get one somewhere else."

Davin made a small sound that might have been a laugh.

Rinna did not.

"Anything else?"

The boy hesitated.

"He asked where you keep it."

Rinna's face changed.

Not fear.

Attention.

"Keep what?"

"Money."

"Exact words."

The boy squeezed his eyes shut.

"Does the woman keep the money at the hall?"

Nobody spoke for a moment.

From the stage, Marek shouted, "I am not limping. The character is limping."

Nessa shouted back, "The character is doing it badly."

The boy looked toward the noise.

Rinna said, "What did Olin answer?"

"He told him to buy oil or leave."

"Did he buy oil?"

"No."

"Did he leave?"

"Yes."

"Did he threaten Olin?"

"No."

"Did he say Bren?"

"No."

"Did he say theatre money was spoken for again?"

"No."

"Did he ask about carts?"

"No."

"Did he ask about Greg?"

The boy looked at me.

"Oil man?"

I closed my eyes.

"Greg," Rinna said.

"No."

Good.

Rinna took a scrap of paper from the shelf and wrote while the boy watched.

MAN RETURNED TO OLIN.

ASKED:
SHE BOUGHT IT ANYWAY?
SHE PAID CASH FOR IT?
STILL DOING SHOWS?
DOES THE WOMAN KEEP THE MONEY AT THE HALL?

OLIN GAVE NO ANSWERS.

She looked at the boy.

"Anything wrong?"

He read slowly.

"He said 'she bought it anyway,' not 'did she.'"

Rinna scratched out the first line and rewrote it.

I liked him.

"Anything else?" she asked.

"No."

"Good. Tell Olin thank you."

The boy did not leave.

Rinna waited.

He shifted his feet.

"I saw him later."

There it was.

I felt the old part of my mind stand up too quickly.

Rinna said, "Where?"

"I had the glass order for the woman near South Steps. He was ahead of me after I came off Narrow Street."

"Doing what?"

"Walking."

"With anyone?"

"No."

"Following anyone?"

"Don't know."

"Which way?"

"Toward Mason's Cut."

My hands tightened on the crutch grips.

Mason's Cut.

Grit on Bren's boot.

A detail I had used before I understood whether it mattered.

Now the same place-name appeared again, carried by a boy who sold lamp oil and had no reason to care about my theories.

I wanted to ask how far.

Which entrance.

Whether the man turned.

Whether he met anyone.

Whether he went into a building.

Whether the boy saw the left side of his coat.

Whether there was mud on his boots.

Rinna said, "You saw him walking toward Mason's Cut."

"Yes."

"Did you see him enter Mason's Cut?"

"No. I turned for South Steps."

"Good."

I hated the word good.

It was correct.

Rinna added:

BOY LATER SAW HIM WALKING TOWARD MASON'S CUT. DID NOT SEE HIM ENTER.

Then she folded the paper once.

"Thank Olin for me."

The boy nodded.

I said, "Wait."

Rinna looked at me.

I knew what she thought I was about to do.

Possibly because I was thinking about doing it.

"I'm not following him."

"Excellent."

"I was going to give the boy bread."

The boy looked interested.

Rinna looked at my bag.

"Your bread?"

I reconsidered the entire moral structure of generosity.

I tore off a piece.

The boy accepted it.

"Thank you, oil man."

"Leave."

He did.

Rinna picked up her handbills again.

I stared at her.

"That's it?"

"No."

"Good."

"You're Landlord today."

I stared harder.

"That is not what I meant."

"I know."

She handed me three pages.

LANDLORD.

Nine lines.

I looked toward the stage where Marek was still practicing the bad limp.

"Which play?"

"The Cousin."

"I haven't done Landlord."

"You have watched it."

"That is not the same thing."

"Correct. Teren wants you in ten minutes."

"What are we doing about the man?"

"Talking to two more people we actually do business with. I am doing that. You are being a landlord."

"He asked where you keep the money."

"Yes."

"That is more specific."

"Yes."

"Mason's Cut."

"He walked toward it."

I exhaled.

"You enjoy this."

"No. I enjoy you not making my paper worse."

Fair.

The Cousin was a stupid play.

This was not criticism either. It knew.

A man pretended to be his own wealthy cousin to avoid paying three separate people. The lie became difficult because the cousin had supposedly rented a room from my character, the Landlord, who had never seen him. Marek played the liar. Hara played his sister. Pell played a creditor with an alarming hat.

My job was mostly to want rent.

I had experience.

Teren put me beside the stage door and ran the scene once.

I entered too early.

"Again," he said.

"I thought the knock was mine."

"It was the creditor."

"There are two knocks."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Doors."

Terrible explanation.

Again.

This time I waited for the second knock and entered correctly.

Marek turned toward me with the broad, desperate smile of a man whose entire life had become paperwork.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

Teren said, "No."

I stopped.

"That is my line."

"You're waiting for it to be funny."

I looked at him.

"It is one word."

"Exactly."

"How do I not wait with one word?"

"Want the rent."

I hated theatre.

Again.

Marek smiled.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

Better.

Not because I changed the word.

Because I interrupted the smile.

Marek reacted faster.

"Of course. My cousin has it."

"Then I want your cousin."

"He is away."

"Then I want the rent."

Teren pointed at me.

"Keep that."

"It is written."

"I know."

Excellent profession.

We worked for another twenty minutes.

I missed a chair on the first turn and clipped it with one crutch. Nessa moved it half a foot and told me not to pretend the chair had attacked.

"It was in my route."

"Your route was wrong."

"Hostile furniture."

"Wrong route."

She won.

By midday Rinna had returned from somewhere with dust on her hem and two fewer handbills.

She did not announce a breakthrough.

She told Jori that the lamp-glass woman would send word if anyone asked about theatre purchases. She told Davin that the cart repair man had been told the same thing. Then she put the remaining handbills back on the shelf and asked whether the front hinge was still sticking.

It was.

We worked on the hinge.

That was the strange part.

The man had asked where the money was kept.

The hinge still needed oil.

Both facts occupied the same building.

By afternoon the house began filling.

The Cousin was paired with a shorter piece I had seen but never performed in. I only had Landlord. Good.

My nine lines did not deserve panic.

I panicked modestly anyway.

The first scenes went cleanly.

Hara got the first real laugh by entering with a basket, taking one look at Marek's fake mustache, and saying nothing for so long that he finally touched it to check whether it had fallen off.

It had not.

The audience understood her entire opinion before she spoke.

When she finally said, "Cousin," the room broke.

Marek almost lost his next line.

Almost.

He recovered by bowing too deeply, which made the mustache lift at one corner.

Hara watched it happen.

Then looked at the audience.

Bigger laugh.

Nothing I did came close.

Good.

My entrance came after the creditor's second knock.

I heard the first.

Waited.

Heard the second.

Entered.

Marek smiled.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

The audience laughed.

Not much.

Enough.

I continued.

Competent.

Ordinary.

Then I made the mistake.

Marek said his cousin had gone to visit an aunt.

My line was, "Then your aunt may pay me."

I said, "Then your cousin may pay me."

Which was the entire problem.

Marek stared at me.

I stared back.

The audience waited.

He said, "He would, if he were not visiting my aunt."

Right.

I could have tried to repair it cleverly.

I did not.

"Then your aunt may pay me."

A small laugh.

The scene continued.

Backstage, Teren caught my sleeve as I passed.

"You repeated him."

"I know."

"Listen."

"I was listening."

"To yourself."

Annoying.

Accurate.

Then he let go because another scene was happening and my personal development was not the theatre's emergency.

Excellent.

The final Landlord scene went better.

No invention.

No rescue.

I entered on the correct knock, wanted rent, did not collide with furniture, and left when the scene ended.

After curtain, the audience became coats and voices and feet moving toward the street.

The company became work again.

Benches shifted.

Props returned to boxes.

Marek peeled off the mustache and stuck it to Pell's sleeve.

Pell did not notice for almost a minute.

Hara did.

She told no one.

I respected her enormously.

Rinna paid me the normal copper.

I put it away.

I did not immediately imagine it crossing Antonius Vale's counter.

Not because the debt had stopped existing.

Because bread existed too.

Soap existed.

Oil existed.

Crutch tips wore down.

Clothes tore.

People who planned to repay debts still had to remain people long enough to do it.

This was obvious.

I had apparently needed several adults to explain it.

Rinna was at the rear table with the folded paper from that morning.

I stopped beside her.

"Any more word?"

"No."

"Did anyone else get asked?"

"Not that I know."

"You're going to keep talking to suppliers?"

"People we actually use."

"Not everyone."

"I don't have time to create a citywide society for people annoyed by strangers."

"Could charge dues."

"Go home."

I looked at the paper.

"The money question matters."

"Yes."

"More than the oil question."

"Maybe."

I smiled.

She saw it.

"Don't."

"You said maybe."

"About importance, not identity."

"The paper survives us being stupid."

"I regret teaching you anything."

"You didn't teach me."

"Worse."

I went home.

Lyssa was not there.

That was becoming normal enough that I did not sit around inventing explanations.

I washed.

The new soap worked offensively well.

I ate some bread.

I considered the copper from the show.

Then put it with the rest of my money.

Not Vale money.

Not food money.

Money.

I could decide what it became when I needed to.

Lyssa arrived near dusk carrying a narrow wrapped bundle under one arm and a small packet in the other.

She put both on the table.

"You bought soap."

"I have been financially reckless."

She looked at me.

"Use more next time."

Cruel.

She unwrapped the smaller packet. Dried fruit.

I forgave her.

"Your day?" she asked.

I told her.

Olin's man returned.

Olin gave him nothing.

The questions.

Oil.

Cash.

Shows.

Where Rinna kept the money.

The boy later saw him walking toward Mason's Cut.

Did not see him enter.

No Bren name.

No threat.

No direct connection proven.

Lyssa ate one piece of fruit.

"And you didn't follow him."

"No."

She looked suspicious.

"I considered it professionally."

"What profession?"

"Landlord."

"What?"

I explained the play.

She laughed at the wrong part, which was apparently me saying the cousin should pay when the entire scene already depended on the cousin not being there.

"It was one line."

"It was the important line."

"There were nine."

"Eight, then."

I took dried fruit before she could become worse.

After a moment she said, "You heard about him before he cost you something this time."

I stopped chewing.

That was true.

Not victory.

Not safety.

Olin had simply done what Rinna asked.

A merchant had refused to answer questions about a customer. A boy had carried a message. Rinna had written down the words. Two more businesses knew how to reach her.

Small things.

Ordinary things.

Useful things.

"Yes," I said.

Lyssa nodded and went back to opening her larger bundle.

Inside was a dark sleeve with three chalk marks near the cuff.

Her work continued too.

No Hessa note came that night.

No one knocked.

Somewhere in Carrow, a thin-faced man in a brown coat had asked where the theatre kept its money.

I did not know where he slept.

I did not know who paid him, if anyone did.

I did not know whether Mason's Cut meant anything beyond the direction he had walked.

But for the first time, he had come looking for information and left without getting it.

We had gotten his questions instead.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
